Give each team its own project for its pipelines and outputs, referencing shared inputs across projects, so ownership is clear
Make one team read-only in the shared project
Merge the two teams' pipelines into one shared pipeline

stem: A restricted view backs an object type. Users report that counts shown in a Workshop aggregation differ from counts in a report built directly on the underlying dataset by the data team. Is this a defect?

choices.text: Yes: the dataset must be rebuilt so that the view matches
Yes: Workshop aggregations are known to be inaccurate on restricted views
Yes: a restricted view must always return the same row counts as the underlying dataset, so a mismatch means the view's policy is broken
Not necessarily: the view returns only each viewer's permitted rows, so their aggregate covers a subset; the difference is expected and should be explained

stem: A regulator asks the team to demonstrate that only authorized users could access a sensitive dataset over the past year. Which evidence can the data engineer assemble?

choices.text: Access configuration history (markings, roles), Check Access results, lineage with controls on derived datasets, and the platform's audit logs
A verbal assurance from the project owner
A list of all users in the organization who, when asked, said that they never opened the dataset during the past year
A screenshot of the current permissions page only

stem: An "Order" object type has 120 properties, including the customer's address fields, the product's specifications and the warehouse's contact details, all copied onto each order. Applications are slow and the data is often inconsistent. What is the modeling problem and fix?

choices.text: There is no modeling problem; wide object types with everything copied on are faster for applications because no link traversals are needed
It is overly broad and duplicates other entities; model Customer, Product and Warehouse as object types linked from Order
Split Order into 12 object types of 10 properties each by column position
Delete the extra properties and keep only the order id

stem: A Patient object type must be linked to Hospital. Each patient is registered at exactly one hospital; each hospital has many patients. The patients dataset has a `hospital_id` column. Which link configuration is correct?

choices.text: A many-to-one link from Patient to Hospital using `hospital_id` on the patient dataset
No link; store the hospital name on the patient as a property
A one-to-one link, since each patient has one hospital
A many-to-many link backed by a separate join dataset of patient and hospital ids maintained by the pipeline

stem: An analyst created an object type "CustomerProduct" with one object per customer-product pair holding the customer's name, the product's name and the number of purchases. Applications now need customer addresses too, and the analyst proposes adding them to CustomerProduct. What should the data engineer advise?

choices.text: Create a new object type CustomerProductAddress
Add the address columns to CustomerProduct, since that is the object type the applications already read and it avoids a model change
Store the address as a JSON string on CustomerProduct
Model Customer and Product as object types with a Purchase relationship holding the count, and put the address on Customer

stem: An object type's property must be renamed, and three Workshop apps and two functions reference it. How should this be approached?

choices.text: Add a second property with the new name alongside the old one and leave both in place forever so that nothing ever needs to be updated
Delete the property and recreate it with the new name
Rename on a Global Branching branch, update the apps and functions there, validate, and merge together
Rename it in place during the day, since renames are instant

stem: The business wants to attach "country" values with a fixed list and consistent display across many object types. Which Ontology construct helps?

choices.text: A separate Country object type linked from every other object type in the Ontology, even where only the label is needed for display
A free-text string property on each object type, trusting pipelines to spell countries consistently
A JSON property holding the country name and code together
A value type or shared property that defines the allowed values and formatting once and is reused

stem: An object type's primary key column has 2% null values in the backing dataset, and those rows do not appear as objects. The analyst wants them included. What is the correct response?

choices.text: Investigate why those rows lack ids, fix identity upstream or derive a deterministic key, and add a non-null expectation
Ask the Ontology to accept null keys
Use the row number as the key for those rows only
Replace the null ids with the string "UNKNOWN" in the transform so that every row has a key value and appears as an object

stem: Which of the following computations is best placed north of the Ontology rather than materialized in the pipeline?

choices.text: The number of open tickets per customer, refreshed hourly
A product's average rating from all reviews, refreshed daily
A what-if delivery date for an order if the user moves it to another warehouse, computed while they edit it in Workshop
Each customer's total spend over the last year, used in list filters and in several dashboards across the company

stem: A team wants to retire an old object type that applications no longer use and replace it with a redesigned one backed by a new dataset. Some users made edits on the old objects. What migration plan is appropriate?

choices.text: Rename the old object type to the new name and point the new dataset at it as its backing, without migrating any of the user edits
Verify consumers with lineage, map old to new by stable key, migrate edits and links, overlap briefly, then deprecate and remove
Delete the old object type immediately, since no application uses it
Keep both object types forever to be safe

stem: A data engineer wants help designing a pipeline's structure and generating boilerplate transforms from a description of the sources and targets. Which AI capability is intended for this?

choices.text: AIP Assist, the platform-wide helper, which can generate a complete pipeline from a description if asked in the right way
An LLM transform, which produces data columns from a prompt
An embedding transform, which converts descriptions into vectors
AI FDE or a code assistant such as Continue, which help engineers author pipelines interactively

stem: An LLM transform extracts a numeric "contract value" from documents. Sometimes the model returns "approximately 1.2M" or "1,200,000 USD". The downstream column is numeric. What should the pipeline do?

choices.text: Convert "approximately" to zero
Ask the model to try harder to return a number
Constrain the schema to a number plus a currency field, normalize residual formatting in code, validate ranges, and flag unparseable rows
Write whatever text the model returns into a string column as is, and let each downstream consumer parse the number in the way that suits it

stem: A legal team wants two things: a risk category on every one of 400,000 historical contracts for reporting, and the ability to ask a specific contract "does this clause allow assignment to a subsidiary?" Which layering is correct?

choices.text: Risk category as a pipeline LLM enrichment stored as a property; the clause question answered interactively at the application layer
Both in the pipeline, including pre-answering every possible clause question
Neither; legal work cannot use AI
Both at the Ontology/application layer, computing the risk category only when a user opens a contract and answering questions in the same function

stem: A code assistant generated a transform that works but reads the same large input three times because it recomputes an intermediate result in three places. What should the engineer do?

choices.text: Ask the assistant to make the transform faster and merge whatever it returns without reading it, since the assistant understands the code best
Review it like any code: compute the intermediate once (or persist it), verify identical output on a branch, and merge
Ship it, since correctness is what matters
Add more executors so the triple read is faster

stem: A pipeline runs an LLM step over new documents nightly. The team wants to measure its ongoing quality without re-labelling everything. What is a practical quality-check design?

choices.text: Validation failure rates, output distribution monitoring, a weekly human-reviewed random sample, and a fixed evaluation set re-run on changes
Trust the model since it was tested once at launch
Re-label every document every night
Ask the model to rate its own confidence on every document and trust that score as the quality measurement, reviewing nothing else

stem: A data engineer is asked to add "semantic search over support tickets" to a Workshop app. Which part of the work belongs to the data engineer's pipeline, and which to the application layer?

choices.text: Everything belongs to the application team; the data engineer only provides the raw dataset
The data engineer should also embed the users' search queries inside the nightly pipeline, since all embedding work is a pipeline concern
Semantic search should be done by re-embedding all tickets at query time in the app
The data engineer builds the embedding pipeline and exposes a vector property on Ticket; the application embeds queries and searches it

stem: An AI assistant proposed a transform that fills missing values in a revenue column with the column's mean "to avoid nulls downstream". The engineer notices this. What should happen?

choices.text: Use the median instead of the mean
Reject it: mean imputation fabricates financial data; preserve and flag the nulls, fix the source, and document the contract
Fill with zero instead
Accept the suggestion, since nulls cause problems in downstream aggregations and the mean is a reasonable estimate of the missing revenue

stem: A pipeline team is deciding whether to use an LLM transform or a deterministic rule set to standardize 50,000 address records with varied formats. What is the sound reasoning?

choices.text: Always use rules, since LLMs are never appropriate in pipelines
Use the LLM for every record and skip validation against reference data, since occasional address errors are low risk and easy to correct later
Deterministic parsing and reference data as the primary method, with an LLM only for the residual records rules cannot parse, validated and audited
Always use the LLM, since it handles variety better than rules

stem: A team must ingest from a SaaS application that offers only a REST API with OAuth authentication and a daily rate limit. Which setup is appropriate?

choices.text: A REST source with OAuth stored in the connection, a sync with pagination and incremental parameters, scheduled within the rate limit
A JDBC connection to the SaaS vendor's internal database, obtained by asking the vendor for direct database credentials and a firewall exception
A manual export from the SaaS interface each week by an analyst, uploaded to Foundry as a spreadsheet for the pipeline to read
A streaming sync that polls the API continuously, so the data is always current regardless of the vendor's rate limit

stem: An append sync keyed on a timestamp column occasionally misses rows that arrived at the source with a timestamp slightly earlier than the previous run's watermark, because the source commits out of order. What is the right mitigation?

choices.text: Ignore the missing rows, since they are a small fraction and will not affect most downstream reports
Ask the source team to stop committing rows out of order, since the sync cannot be expected to handle it
Switch to a full snapshot every run, since the only way to guarantee completeness is to copy the whole table every time
Use a lookback window: re-read rows from a little before the last watermark and deduplicate on the primary key

stem: An auditor asks which external destinations data can be exported to from the platform and who approved them. What should the data engineer be able to show?

choices.text: A list compiled from memory by the engineers who have set up exports in the past year
Nothing, since exports are configured by individual users for their own purposes and the platform does not track or approve them centrally
The configured egress policies and export destinations with approval records, plus the execution history of exports
The outbound firewall logs of the company network, which show every connection made by the platform

stem: A sync's execution history shows every run succeeding with zero records for the past week, while the source team confirms thousands of new rows. What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: The source team is mistaken, and no new rows actually exist in the table
The sync's incremental condition or filter no longer matches new rows (a watermark reset, a status value the source stopped using)
The agent has silently stopped forwarding data while still reporting success for every run
The dataset has reached a storage limit on the platform and silently rejects new transactions without reporting an error to the sync

stem: Sensor data arrives as thousands of small JSON files per hour landing in a cloud object storage bucket. Analysts need the data within about 15 minutes. Which ingestion fits?

choices.text: A virtual table over the bucket so that analysts query the JSON files in place without ingestion
A streaming sync from the bucket, since the files arrive continuously and only streaming can meet the latency
A frequent file sync (every 10 minutes) that picks up new files and appends them, with downstream compaction
A nightly file sync that copies the day's files in one transaction, since object storage sources are batch sources

stem: Which statement about change-data-capture (CDC) ingestion is correct?

choices.text: CDC is the simplest sync pattern and should be used by default for every table because it requires no configuration on the source side
CDC can only capture inserts, so deletes and updates still require a periodic snapshot to be reflected downstream
CDC produces a current-state table directly, so no downstream transform is needed to apply the changes
CDC reads the source's change log to replicate inserts, updates and deletes, capturing changes without needing a timestamp column

stem: A virtual table over an external warehouse has become slow for analysts, and the warehouse team reports high query costs from Foundry. What should be done?

choices.text: Review the queries (pushdown, columns, joins), add filters, and materialize a curated subset in Foundry for common analyses if policy allows
Delete the virtual table, since virtual tables are only meant for one-off exploration and should never be used by multiple analysts at the same time
Switch all analysts to querying the warehouse directly with their own credentials instead of through Foundry
Increase the warehouse's compute size so that the queries complete faster regardless of their shape

stem: A data engineer is designing ingestion for a new source and wants to avoid the problems seen on earlier syncs: silent empty runs, stale data unnoticed, and agent outages. What should be built in from the start?

choices.text: A second redundant sync of the same source so that if one fails the other provides the data
Status, freshness and size health checks, a minimum-row expectation where appropriate, agent health monitoring, alert routing and runbooks
A daily email to the whole team listing every sync's record counts so that someone can notice problems
Nothing extra; the earlier problems were specific to those particular sources and their agents, and they are unlikely to recur with a new one

stem: A dataset has one row per sensor reading with a timestamp. The business wants, per sensor, the difference between each reading and the previous reading. Which transformation construct is appropriate?

choices.text: A group-by aggregation on sensor id that returns the minimum and maximum readings, from which the differences can be inferred
A window function partitioned by sensor and ordered by timestamp that provides the previous reading (lag) so the difference is computed per row
A self-join of the dataset to itself on sensor id, which pairs every reading with every other reading of the same sensor for comparison
A Python loop over the rows collected to the driver that keeps the previous reading in a variable and writes the difference out

stem: An analyst built a working transformation in a Contour analysis and wants it to become a scheduled production dataset consumed by other teams. What should the data engineer do?

choices.text: Export the analysis result to a spreadsheet each night and upload it as the production dataset
Schedule the Contour analysis to refresh nightly and point the consuming teams at its result, since the logic is already proven correct
Tell the consumers to rerun the Contour analysis themselves whenever they need fresh data
Re-implement it as a governed pipeline with expectations, lineage and a schedule, using the Contour analysis as the specification

stem: A Spark transform processes a 2 TB input, but one stage spends most of its time on a single task while the others finish quickly. What is the likely cause and remedy?

choices.text: Data skew on a join or group key; repartition or salt the hot key, or broadcast a small side, confirmed in Spark details
A slow disk on one node; the fix is to request new hardware from the platform team
Insufficient executors overall; the fix is to double the executor count so that every stage, including the slow one, finishes sooner
Too many input files; the fix is to delete the smallest files from the input dataset

stem: A pipeline must enrich each customer with the latest known address from a change-history table that holds every address a customer has ever had, with effective dates. Which transformation produces the correct "current address"?

choices.text: A join on customer id and the current date, which matches the address row whose effective date equals today
An inner join of customers to the history table on customer id, which attaches the address
A window ranking addresses per customer by effective date, keeping the latest, then a left join of customers to that dataset
A group-by on customer id selecting the maximum address string, which returns the latest alphabetically

stem: A code transform's output must satisfy a contract that downstream teams rely on: specific columns, types and no nulls in keys. How should the contract be enforced in the pipeline?

choices.text: A detailed comment at the top of the transform describing the contract for other engineers to read before they change anything
A unit test that checks the transform's code compiles, which guarantees the output shape
A monthly review meeting where downstream teams confirm the output still looks right
Schema expectations (columns, types) and non-null key expectations on the output that fail the build, with the contract documented

stem: A transform's input is 200 GB today and expected to reach 5 TB within a year. It currently runs on a lightweight single-node engine and is close to its memory limit. What should be planned?

choices.text: Split the input into 25 separate datasets of 200 GB each and run 25 copies of the lightweight transform
Migrate the transform to a distributed engine (Spark) now, validating output equivalence on a branch, so the pipeline scales with the projected growth
Keep the lightweight engine and request progressively larger single nodes as the data grows, since single-node processing is simpler to maintain
Sample the input to 10% permanently so that the lightweight engine always has enough memory

stem: A transform occasionally produces slightly different outputs on identical inputs: row order varies and a "first value per group" column changes. Downstream equality checks fail intermittently. What is the cause and fix?

choices.text: Non-deterministic logic: "first" without explicit ordering depends on partitioning; add a sort key with a tie-breaker to ordered selections
The input changing between runs, fixed by snapshotting the input before each run
A platform bug; open a support ticket and wait for a fix before running the transform again
Insufficient executor memory causing some rows to be dropped at random during the shuffle, fixed by increasing memory per executor

stem: A pipeline mixes three concerns in one transform: parsing a messy source, applying business rules, and producing an Ontology-ready dataset. Changes are risky and reviews are slow. How should it be restructured?

choices.text: Duplicate the transform per consuming team so each team can edit its own copy without affecting the others
Move all three concerns into a single Pipeline Builder pipeline with no intermediate datasets so that there is only one place to look
Split into staged transforms with contracts: parsing to a typed dataset, business rules to curated data, Ontology shaping, each with expectations
Keep one transform but add many comments so that reviewers can follow the three concerns within it

stem: A regulatory report is produced from a 3-year transaction history every month-end. Inputs are final by the 2nd of the month. Which processing mode is appropriate for the report transform?

choices.text: A scheduled monthly batch that runs after the inputs are final, recomputing the report from the full history
Hourly incremental processing throughout the month, so that the report is already complete and waiting on the 1st before inputs are final
A lightweight single-node transform run by hand whenever someone remembers that the report is due
Streaming, so that the report is continuously up to date and ready the moment the month ends

stem: A dataset consumer complains that a row they deleted from the source still appears in Foundry a week later. The sync is append-only. What is happening?

choices.text: The agent is caching rows and must be restarted to clear the deleted row from Foundry
The Ontology keeps deleted rows for audit and they cannot be removed from the dataset
The deletion will appear automatically in Foundry after the dataset's default retention period of 30 days expires and the row ages out
An append-only sync never removes rows; deletions need CDC with deletes, periodic snapshots, or a soft-delete flag

stem: A streaming pipeline must guarantee that each sensor event affects the aggregate exactly once, even though the source may redeliver messages after network errors. Which design provides this?

choices.text: Restarting the streaming pipeline whenever a duplicate is suspected so that its state is rebuilt from scratch and any duplicate is forgotten
Counting every message as received, since duplicates are rare and cancel out over time
Deduplication on a unique event id within a bounded window, with idempotent updates to the aggregate keyed on that id
Trusting the source, since message brokers never deliver a message more than once

stem: An upstream team wants to switch their dataset from daily APPEND transactions to a daily SNAPSHOT because it is "simpler". Three incremental transforms depend on it. What should the data engineer explain?

choices.text: The switch is fine as long as the snapshot is taken at night when the consumers are not running
All three consumers would fall back to full recompute daily; if snapshots are truly needed, consumers must redesign, so the change must be coordinated
Snapshots are illegal for datasets that have incremental consumers, so the request must be refused
Nothing changes for consumers, since the data content is the same either way and the transaction type is an internal detail of the upstream team

stem: A team wants metrics on website events with a 5-minute freshness requirement during business hours and no requirement overnight. Events arrive as a stream. What is a cost-aware design?

choices.text: A full batch transform every 5 minutes around the clock over the entire event history
A streaming or micro-batch pipeline for live metrics in business hours, with overnight batch consolidation for historical aggregates
Nightly batch only, telling the business that 5-minute freshness is not achievable on a stream of this volume without unreasonable cost
A lightweight transform every minute over all history, since lightweight engines are cheap

stem: After a streaming pipeline was changed to add a new field, records from before the change lack the field and downstream code fails on them. How should schema evolution have been handled?

choices.text: By rejecting any record that lacks the field, since the schema now requires it
By converting the pipeline to batch, which handles schema changes automatically
By clearing the stream and its retained history and starting over, so that only records carrying the new field ever exist in the pipeline
By making the new field optional in the schema and downstream code so old and new records coexist, with a backfill or default where needed

stem: An incremental transform should process late corrections to already-processed days without reprocessing the entire history. The source delivers corrections as APPEND files tagged with the day they correct. Which design works?

choices.text: Keyed, idempotent processing: output partitioned by day and key, with a correction's day tag directing the merge to that day's partition
Switch to a full snapshot transform so every correction triggers a complete recompute
Ignore the day tags and append corrections as new rows, letting consumers figure out for themselves which rows are corrections of which
Reject corrections older than the previous run, since incremental transforms cannot modify past output

stem: A dataset receives a DELETE transaction removing last month's files for data-retention reasons. A downstream incremental transform keeps a running total. What is the correct consequence and handling?

choices.text: The transform will crash and must be deleted and rebuilt from scratch
The running total should remain unchanged because retention deletions are administrative and should not affect any computed values downstream
The transform falls back to a full recompute over retained files; totals that must include deleted periods need a rollup materialized before deletion
The DELETE will be ignored by the transform because incremental transforms only read APPEND transactions

stem: A dataset is rebuilt by its schedule even on days when its only input has not changed, wasting compute. Which schedule setting addresses this?

choices.text: Configuring the schedule to build only when the input has a new transaction since the last successful build
Reducing the dataset's executor size so that the unnecessary builds at least cost less compute than before
Moving the schedule to a later hour so that the input is more likely to have changed by the time the build runs each day
Removing the schedule and asking the consuming team to trigger a build manually whenever they need fresh data

stem: A build failed and the error message says a column referenced by the transform does not exist in the input. The transform's code has not changed. What should the engineer check first?

choices.text: The schedule, since a column may be missing if the build ran before the input finished writing
The input's latest schema against the previous transaction, since an upstream rename or drop is likely with unchanged code
The executor memory, since schema errors are sometimes a symptom of running out of memory during parsing
The transform's code for typos in column names, since a missing column error almost always means a mistake in the column reference

stem: An on-call engineer receives an alert that a critical dataset's build failed at 03:00. Which sequence matches the troubleshooting playbook?

choices.text: Roll back the transform's code to last week's version, since recent code changes are the most common cause of failures
Escalate to the data owner and wait for the morning, since builds that fail at night are usually fixed by the next scheduled run
Read the symptom, find the first failing stage via lineage and logs, classify it, repair minimally, rebuild, verify
Immediately force-rebuild the dataset, and if that fails, force-rebuild all of its upstream datasets as well

stem: A team wants to be able to restore a dataset to yesterday's state quickly if a bad build publishes wrong data. What capability should they rely on?

choices.text: Nothing, since once a build publishes, the previous data is gone and cannot be recovered
A duplicate copy of the dataset maintained by a second, identical pipeline that runs one day behind the first so yesterday's state always exists
A nightly manual export of the dataset to a file share so that it can be re-uploaded if needed
The dataset's transaction history: earlier transactions remain available, so it can be restored and downstream rebuilt

stem: A build fails with a permission error reading a dataset that it read successfully yesterday. No permissions were intentionally changed. What should be investigated?

choices.text: Whether the transform code was modified to reference a different dataset, since permission errors are usually caused by code changes
Whether the dataset was deleted and recreated, which resets the file paths and causes permission errors
Whether the cluster was restarted overnight, which temporarily revokes build permissions
Whether a marking was newly applied upstream or the build identity's group membership changed, using Check Access to pinpoint the requirement

stem: Two independent pipelines read the same large input and both run at 02:00, competing for compute and slowing each other down. Both must finish by 06:00. What is a reasonable scheduling adjustment?

choices.text: Merge the two pipelines into one transform so that only one job runs
Give both pipelines the maximum executor count so that each gets as much compute as possible
Stagger or sequence them (one triggered on the other's completion, or a different time) so they do not contend, and verify the window
Schedule both at 00:00 so that they have more time before the deadline, even though they will still compete with each other for compute

stem: A pipeline must be modified by a contractor who should not be able to merge changes into production without review. How should repository permissions and workflow be set?

choices.text: Let the contractor create branches and pull requests, require a team member's approval before merging, and restrict direct writes to main
Give the contractor full edit rights on the main branch and trust them to request a review before merging
Let the contractor work directly on main during a scheduled window when the team is watching
Give the contractor no repository access at all and have them send code changes by email for a team member to paste in and commit

stem: A dataset's build succeeds but takes twice as long every Monday. Spark details show the Monday runs read many more input files. What is the cause and the fix?

choices.text: Monday data is larger; nothing can be done except accepting the longer build
The weekend's incremental syncs accumulate many small files the Monday build must read; compact the input and write larger files
The transform has a bug that only triggers on Mondays; the fix is to add a day-of-week condition to the code
Monday builds are slower because the cluster is busy catching up after the weekend; the fix is to move the build to Tuesday morning

stem: A dataset must never contain rows where `end_date` is before `start_date`. Such rows have appeared twice from a source bug. Which control is appropriate?

choices.text: A transform that swaps the two dates when they are reversed, which corrects the source bug automatically
A build-blocking expectation asserting `end_date >= start_date` for every row, since a violation must never be published
A note in the dataset description warning consumers that date ordering is not guaranteed
A health check that counts such rows after each build and alerts the owner so they can fix them in the source eventually

stem: A content health check on null rate started alerting daily after a new, legitimately optional column was added to the dataset. What should be done?

choices.text: Fill the optional column with empty strings so that the null rate drops back below the threshold
Ignore the alerts, since everyone knows the new column is optional
Remove the null-rate check entirely, since it clearly cannot handle datasets that contain optional columns alongside required ones
Scope the check to columns where nulls matter, with column-specific thresholds, and document that the new column is optional

stem: An expectation on a referential rule (every order's `customer_id` must exist in the customers dataset) fails whenever the customer feed lags the order feed by a few hours. Orders are legitimate and the customers arrive later. What is a sound design?

choices.text: Remove the referential expectation, since timing differences make it impossible to enforce
Insert placeholder customers for the missing ids so the expectation passes
Keep the rule on the published dataset; stage orders whose customers have not arrived in a pending dataset, and sequence customers first
Drop the orders whose customers have not arrived yet, since the pipeline cannot publish invalid data and those orders can be re-sent

stem: A dataset's schema health check fired because a new column was added by the upstream team as planned. The team wants future planned additions not to alert but unexpected changes still to. What should they configure?

choices.text: Alert on removed or retyped columns while allowing additive ones, and update the expected schema for planned changes as part of release
Set the check to alert only once a month so that planned changes are batched
Disable the schema check, since planned changes are now common and the alerts are no longer useful
Have the upstream team stop adding columns altogether, since schema stability for consumers is more important than any new fields

stem: A business rule states that order amounts must be positive except for refunds, and that refund amounts must not exceed the original order's amount. Which combination enforces these?

choices.text: Documentation of the rules in the dataset description for consumers to verify themselves
A row-level expectation for the sign rule, plus a transform-computed cross-row flag (refund vs original) with an expectation that it is never true
A single expectation that the total of all refunds is less than the total of all orders across the whole dataset, checked on every build
Two health checks that alert when violations appear in the published dataset

stem: Freshness alerts for a dataset fire every Monday morning because the source does not deliver on weekends. What is the right change?

choices.text: Replace the freshness check with a build-status check, which does not care about delivery days and therefore cannot fire on Monday mornings
Ask the source to deliver on weekends so the check can stay as it is
Set the freshness threshold to the source's real delivery calendar (a longer window over weekends, or a schedule-aware check)
Disable the freshness check on Mondays, which is the only day it fires

stem: An expectation failure blocks a build at night, and the on-call engineer confirms the data is wrong at the source. The business asks for the dashboard to be updated anyway. What is the right response?

choices.text: Keep the previous good data published, explain that known-bad data would mislead, escalate to the source owner, publish after the fix
Delete the bad rows and publish the rest without telling anyone
Override the expectation and publish the new data, since the business asked for it explicitly and they are the owners of the dashboard
Publish the bad data with a note in the dashboard title saying it may be wrong

stem: A team wants to detect subtle corruption where values are present and typed correctly but wrong (for example, a currency conversion applied twice). Which monitoring approach can catch this?

choices.text: Row-count checks, since corruption usually changes the number of rows
Build-status checks, since corrupt transforms fail to build
Schema checks, since any corruption of the values would also change the data types of the affected columns in a detectable way
Statistical content checks (amount distribution, ratios between related columns, reconciliation against a source total) with alerts

stem: Which of the following correctly describes the difference between a marking and a project role?

choices.text: A marking is a mandatory, data-following control required in addition to any role; a project role is a discretionary permission within a project
Markings and roles are interchangeable ways to grant access, and either one alone is sufficient for a user to read a dataset
A marking applies only to Ontology objects, while roles apply only to datasets and transforms within projects
A marking is a project-scoped permission such as Viewer or Editor, while a role is an organization-wide label that restricts access to sensitive data

stem: A data engineering team supports five business domains. Each domain has its own data sources, curated outputs and consumers. How should projects be organized to keep ownership and permissions manageable?

choices.text: A single platform-wide project containing all five domains, with every dataset's permissions set individually by the engineer who created it
Per-domain project sets (datasource, pipeline, curated) with the domain's owners and consumers as roles, plus a shared reference project
One project per engineer, so that each engineer has full control over the resources they personally created
One project per dataset across all domains, which provides the finest-grained control possible

stem: A dataset of employee records must be readable row-by-row only by each employee's own manager, and HR must see all rows. Which control expresses this?

choices.text: A marking per manager applied to the whole dataset, so each manager must hold their own marking to open it
Separate datasets per manager produced by the pipeline, plus a full dataset for HR, each in its own project
A Workshop filter defaulting to the manager's own team, with HR removing the filter when they need all rows
A restricted view with a policy granting a row when the viewer is the row's manager or a member of the HR group

stem: A pipeline's build identity was granted a marking last month to read a sensitive source. A review asks whether the derived curated dataset is also marked. What should the data engineer verify and why?

choices.text: That the build identity still holds the marking, which is all the review is concerned with
Nothing; markings apply only to the original source dataset and never to datasets derived from it by transforms in other projects
That the curated dataset carries the marking, or was deliberately de-identified and reviewed, traced with lineage
That the curated dataset is in the same project as the source, which makes marking unnecessary

stem: A new user cannot see a project at all in the platform, although they have been added as a Viewer on it. Colleagues in the same team can see it. What is a likely cause?

choices.text: Viewers cannot see projects; only Editors and Owners can
The user belongs to a different organization than the project, so the organization boundary blocks visibility regardless of role
The user has not refreshed their browser session since being added, and project visibility only updates after a full restart of the client
The project is too large to be displayed for new users until it is indexed

stem: A team proposes granting the "Everyone" group Viewer access to their curated project "to reduce access requests". What should the data engineer consider?

choices.text: Agree without conditions, since curated data is by definition safe to share with the whole company
Refuse, since no project should ever be readable by more than one team
Agree but remove all markings from the project's datasets first so that the broad Viewer access actually works for every dataset in it
Evaluate sensitivity: broad read may suit non-sensitive curated data, markings and restricted views keep their controls, and the owner approves

stem: After a dataset was moved from one project to another, a downstream team's scheduled build began failing with an access error. What happened?

choices.text: The dataset now inherits the new project's roles; the build identity had access via the old project and needs a grant in the new one
Moving a dataset between projects deletes its transaction history, so the downstream build has no committed transaction to read from
The downstream transform's code references the old project path and must be rewritten
Dataset moves are not supported and the dataset must be recreated in the original project

stem: A restricted view is used for row-level access, but the team also needs a downstream transform to compute totals across all rows for an unrestricted aggregate dataset that everyone may see. How should this be designed?

choices.text: Have the transform take the restricted view as its input under the build identity, so that the totals reflect whatever rows the policy happens to allow
Remove the restricted view so the transform can read all rows, accepting that every user will then see all rows as well
Read the underlying dataset with a properly granted build identity, compute aggregates, and publish them after a disclosure review
Have every user compute the totals themselves from the rows they can see, then compare their subtotals in a shared spreadsheet

stem: A logistics company needs to model that a Shipment passes through several Hubs in a specific order, with the arrival time at each hub. Which model captures this correctly?

choices.text: A property on Hub recording the most recent shipment that passed through, updated by the pipeline as shipments move
A ShipmentHubVisit object type with sequence number and arrival time, linked to both Shipment and Hub
A list property on Shipment containing the hub names in order, with another list property holding the arrival times in the same order
A many-to-many link between Shipment and Hub with no properties, since the order can be inferred from the hubs' locations on a map

stem: A Product object type uses the product name as its primary key. Two different products were given the same name by marketing, and now their objects have merged, mixing their orders. What is the lesson and fix?

choices.text: Names are not stable identifiers; migrate the key to the SKU or catalogue id with a mapping of edits and links, and add a uniqueness expectation
Add the product's colour and size to the name so that the combined string is unique for every product currently in the catalogue
Rename one product so that the names are unique again, which separates the objects without any model change
Delete both products and recreate them under new names chosen to be distinct

stem: Analysts want an object type "MonthlyRegionSales" with properties for revenue, units and top product per region per month. Is this acceptable, and under what conditions?

choices.text: No; the analysts should recompute the aggregates in each dashboard from the Sale objects every time
Yes, but only if the aggregate replaces the Sale object type entirely, to avoid any duplication of sales data inside the Ontology
Yes, as a derived object type keyed by its grain (region × month), documented as computed from Sales and kept alongside Sale
No; aggregates must never be object types, since the Ontology only models real-world entities

stem: An Ontology change needs both a new object type and a change to the pipeline that produces its backing dataset. How should the two be developed and released together?

choices.text: Create the object type first against an empty dataset, then change the pipeline on main and let the object type populate when the build runs
Develop both directly on main during a maintenance window announced to users
Release the pipeline change first to production, then create the object type a week later once the dataset looks right
Use Global Branching spanning the pipeline and the Ontology resources, develop both on the branch, validate, and merge together

stem: Two object types, Invoice and Payment, each have an "amount" property with different currencies and rounding conventions in their sources, causing confusion in applications. What modeling improvement helps?

choices.text: Convert all amounts to a single reporting currency in the pipeline and store them as plain integers without any currency information
Define a shared monetary value type (currency code plus normalized decimal) for both properties, with pipelines normalizing to it
Rename the properties to amount_invoice and amount_payment so users can tell them apart
Store the amount as a free-text string that includes the currency symbol as it appears in the source

stem: A link between Employee and Department must support the fact that an employee can move between departments over time, and applications need to know the current department and the history. How should this be modeled?

choices.text: A many-to-many link between Employee and Department with no dates, since the history is implied by the set of linked departments
A single many-to-one link from Employee to Department, overwritten each time the employee moves
A list of department names on the Employee object in chronological order
An EmployeeDepartmentAssignment object type with start and end dates linked to both, plus a derived current-department link on Employee

stem: A property "risk score" is computed from an object's own attributes by a formula that changes weekly as the risk team tunes it, and must be applied consistently in reports. Where should it be computed?

choices.text: Nowhere; the risk team should calculate scores in a spreadsheet
In each report separately, so that report owners can apply the formula they prefer
South of the Ontology, in the pipeline, with the formula version recorded, so every consumer sees the same score
North of the Ontology, in a function called by each application when it displays the object, so the latest formula always applies

stem: After changing a property's type from string to integer on a live object type, several Workshop filters and a function broke. What should the engineer have done, and what now?

choices.text: Treated it as breaking: found consumers, changed type and consumers together on a branch; now revert or hot-fix, then redo properly
Nothing could have prevented it; property type changes always break consumers in some way and must simply be done quickly to limit the damage
Kept the type as string forever, since type changes are never worth the risk
Changed the type only at night when fewer users were affected

stem: A data engineer needs embeddings for product descriptions to power semantic search, and also wants to generate short marketing tags for each product. Which capabilities apply?

choices.text: An embedding transform in the pipeline for the vectors and an LLM transform for the tags, both producing columns at build time
A code assistant for both, which computes the vectors and tags and writes them into the dataset during the engineer's coding session
An agent that users ask for each product's embedding and tags whenever they need them
AIP Assist for both, since it can produce vectors and tags when asked in the chat interface

stem: An LLM transform that extracts dates from documents returns them in mixed formats ("3/4/2026", "4 March 2026", "2026-03-04"). The downstream column is a date type. What should the pipeline do?

choices.text: Guess day-first for all ambiguous dates, since most of the documents come from Europe
Drop any row whose date is not already in ISO format
Ask for ISO-8601 in the schema, parse deterministically, validate the date and range, and flag ambiguous forms like 3/4/2026 for review
Store the strings exactly as the model returned them and let each consumer interpret the dates in whichever way suits their own use

stem: Which of the following is an example of AI that belongs at the Ontology/application layer rather than in the pipeline?

choices.text: Translating every product description into four languages in a nightly build so the catalogue is always available in each language
A support agent asking "summarize this customer's complaints this month" while viewing the customer, answered on demand from current tickets
Classifying every incoming document into a document type for routing
Computing an embedding for every support ticket as it arrives

stem: A team adopts a code assistant for writing transforms. Which practice keeps quality high?

choices.text: Ban the assistant for production code and allow it only for notebooks
Let the assistant also review its own code, which replaces human review
Accept generated code whenever it builds successfully, since the assistant has been trained on far more code than the whole team has ever written
Treat generated code as a draft: review assumptions and scale-safety, run tests and branch builds, compare outputs, and keep the engineer accountable

stem: An LLM enrichment runs over sensitive customer notes. Which measures address data protection in the pipeline step itself?

choices.text: Confirm model enablement for the data class, minimize and redact what is sent, keep prompts and responses under the source's markings, record versions
Use the cheapest available model to reduce the exposure window
None, since the model provider is responsible for protecting any data sent to it
Send the full notes to the model as they are but delete the raw responses immediately after parsing so that nothing sensitive is retained

stem: A pipeline enrichment with an LLM costs more than the rest of the platform usage combined. Most of the input rows are unchanged day to day, and the prompt changes rarely. What is the first optimization?

choices.text: Run the enrichment weekly instead of daily so the cost is spread over more days
Switch to a much smaller model and accept whatever quality results from it
Cache results keyed by input content and prompt version so unchanged rows are skipped, and process only new or changed rows
Remove the enrichment from the pipeline entirely, since AI steps are inherently too expensive to run in production pipelines at this scale

stem: A code assistant generated a transform with a hard-coded list of 50 category names copied from the prompt. The categories change monthly. What should the engineer do before merging?

choices.text: Keep the hard-coded list in the transform but add a comment recording the date it was last updated and who is responsible for refreshing it
Replace the hard-coded list with a reference dataset the transform reads, so changes flow through data, and add a test for unknown categories
Merge it and update the list by hand each month when the categories change
Ask the assistant to regenerate the code each month with the new list

stem: A manager proposes using an AI assistant to "automatically fix" pipeline failures by letting it edit and redeploy transforms whenever a build fails. What is the sound response?

choices.text: Agree, provided the assistant is told to be careful in its system prompt
Agree, since faster fixes are always better for the business and the assistant can read error messages and stack traces more quickly than people
Agree, but only for failures that happen at night when no engineer is available
Decline automatic production edits: let the assistant diagnose and propose fixes on a branch, with human review, tests and branch validation before release

stem: A source system exposes its data only through nightly compressed archive files placed in a cloud bucket, each containing dozens of CSV files. Which ingestion design handles this cleanly?

choices.text: A file sync that lands the archives as raw files, followed by a transform that unpacks and parses the CSVs into typed datasets with expectations
A streaming sync that reads each archive byte by byte as it arrives and emits the rows as messages for downstream consumers
A manual process in which an engineer downloads each archive, unzips it on a laptop and uploads the CSVs one by one through the browser
A JDBC sync against the bucket, since cloud buckets can be queried with SQL once the archives have been mounted as tables

stem: An update sync uses a `modified_at` column, but the source stores it in local time with daylight-saving changes. Twice a year, rows go missing or duplicate around the clock change. What is the robust fix?

choices.text: Run a full snapshot on the two days a year when the clocks change and keep the update sync for the rest of the year
Ask analysts to ignore any anomalies that appear in the data during the weeks after a clock change
Use a timezone-independent signal (a UTC timestamp or a monotonic version number), or a lookback window with deduplication
Pause the sync for the hour of the clock change so that no rows are processed during the ambiguous period

stem: A partner needs a daily extract of a curated dataset, but only three of its twelve columns and only rows for their own region. How should the export be designed?

choices.text: Email the partner a spreadsheet each morning prepared by an analyst who filters the data by hand
Give the partner a Foundry account with Viewer access to the curated dataset so they can filter it themselves
Export the full twelve-column dataset to the partner and ask them in the contract to use only the columns and rows they are entitled to
Build a partner-specific dataset with exactly the permitted columns and rows, and export it through a governed export under the egress policy

stem: A sync's schema changed when the source added a column, and the sync now fails with a schema mismatch error. What is the correct handling?

choices.text: Ignore the failure and wait, since the sync will adapt to the new schema automatically after a few runs
Classify the change as additive, update the sync's expected schema, verify downstream transforms on a branch, and rerun the sync
Delete the dataset and recreate it so that the new schema is inferred from scratch, accepting the loss of transaction history
Ask the source team to remove the new column so that the existing sync configuration continues to work unchanged

stem: A new team member asks how Data Connection agents work before planning ingestion from an on-premises database. Which statement about agents is accurate?

choices.text: An agent is software installed inside the customer's network that connects to local sources and communicates outbound to the platform
An agent replaces the need for source credentials entirely, since it authenticates to every source using the platform's own identity
An agent is only required for streaming sources with continuous message flow and is never used for ordinary batch database syncs
An agent is a cloud service run by the platform that pulls data from any source over the public internet without customer involvement

stem: A team must ingest a reference table of 2,000 rows that changes a few times a month, from a database that supports CDC but at significant setup effort. Which pattern is proportionate?

choices.text: Set up CDC despite the effort, since it is the most capable pattern and guarantees every change is captured within seconds of occurring
A streaming sync so that the reference table is updated the instant any row changes
An append sync, since reference tables only ever gain rows
A daily or more frequent snapshot sync, since the table is tiny, changes rarely, and a full copy is cheap and always correct

stem: Analysts querying a virtual table report that results differ from what the warehouse team sees for "the same query". What is a likely explanation to check first?

choices.text: The warehouse team is reading the wrong database or schema on their side and should be corrected before anything else is investigated
The queries differ: Foundry may apply filters, permissions or type coercions, or the data changed between runs; compare the exact query and timing
Virtual tables return randomized samples of the source for performance, so differences between the two sides are expected and unimportant
Virtual tables cache the source data for a week after the first query, so Foundry shows stale results by design until the cache expires

stem: An organization has 300 syncs. The data engineering team wants to find systemic ingestion problems rather than reacting to each failure. What should they build?

choices.text: A rule that every sync failure is emailed immediately to the head of data engineering for personal attention and follow-up
A policy of automatically retrying every failed sync up to ten times, which resolves most failures without any human involvement at all
A monitoring view over execution history and health checks: failure rates by source and agent, lateness distributions, trends, reviewed regularly
A reduction in the number of syncs to a manageable fifty by asking business teams which sources they can do without

stem: A dataset has a column of free-text addresses. The business wants structured city, postal code and country columns. Which transformation approach is appropriate?

choices.text: Splitting the string on commas and assuming the parts are always city, postal code and country in that order
Asking each consuming team to parse the addresses themselves in their own pipelines
Reference-backed address parsing with an LLM step for the residual, postal codes validated against reference lists, and flags for unparseable rows
A single regular expression applied in an expression node, since addresses worldwide follow one consistent pattern that a pattern can capture

stem: A team maintains the same cleaning logic in a Pipeline Builder pipeline and in a code transform for different projects, and the two have drifted apart. What should be done?

choices.text: Consolidate: implement the cleaning once as a shared stage (a published dataset or a code library) and have both projects consume it
Accept the drift, since each project's needs are slightly different anyway
Delete the code transform and tell the second project to copy the Pipeline Builder pipeline manually into their own project whenever it changes
Keep both implementations and add a comment in each pointing to the other, so that future changes are remembered to be made in both places

stem: A Spark transform works on a sample but fails with out-of-memory on the full data during a `collect()` used to build a Python dictionary for lookups. What is the right change?

choices.text: Run the transform on a lightweight single-node engine instead, which has no separate driver limit to run out of during the collect
Reduce the full dataset to a sample permanently so the collect succeeds
Increase the driver memory in the transform's configuration until the collected lookup data fits, and raise it again as the data grows
Replace the collect-and-dictionary pattern with a distributed join (or a broadcast join if the lookup side is small), keeping data in the engine

stem: A transform computes a financial measure whose definition is agreed with finance. How should the definition be protected against accidental change?

choices.text: A lock on the repository that prevents anyone from ever editing the transform again, so that the agreed definition cannot drift
Unit tests encoding the definition, an expectation reconciling the output to a control figure, and required review on changes to the transform
A quarterly check by the finance team of whether the published number still looks right compared with their own ledger
A verbal agreement with the engineer who wrote the transform that they will not change the measure's logic without asking finance first

stem: Two datasets must be joined on customer name because no shared identifier exists, and names have inconsistent casing, punctuation and spacing. What should the transform do?

choices.text: Ask both source teams to add a shared customer identifier to their systems before any join is attempted in the pipeline
Use a fuzzy match on the raw names with no similarity threshold, so that every row in the first dataset finds some partner in the second
Normalize both sides into a join key (case, punctuation, whitespace, abbreviations), join, measure the match rate, and route the unmatched to review
Join on the raw names as they appear in each dataset and accept that rows whose names do not match exactly are lost from the output

stem: Which workload is best served by a lightweight (single-node) transform rather than Spark?

choices.text: A one-off backfill over five years of clickstream data to recompute session metrics with a corrected definition
A nightly join of two tables of about 500 GB each on a customer key, producing a wide output consumed by several teams
A streaming aggregation over millions of sensor events per hour, producing per-device windows with sub-minute latency
A daily transform that reads a 30 MB configuration file, applies validation rules and writes a small lookup table for other pipelines

stem: A transform's output is correct, but reviewers cannot tell why certain rows were filtered out because the filtering logic is spread across several nested expressions. What refactoring helps?

choices.text: Restructuring the logic into named steps, or a reason column recording why each row was excluded, so exclusions are explicit and testable
Removing the filters entirely so that all rows pass through to the output and reviewers have nothing left to question about exclusions
Moving all the filters into a single very long expression at the end of the transform so that they are at least gathered in one place
Adding a long comment at the end of the transform explaining the filters in prose

stem: A team wants to migrate a critical Pipeline Builder pipeline to code to add unit tests and custom logic. How should the migration be done safely?

choices.text: Rewrite it in code but skip the output comparison with the original, since the code version has unit tests and those are sufficient
Rebuild it in code on a branch, compare both implementations' outputs on the same inputs, add tests, then switch consumers with rollback
Keep both the Pipeline Builder and the code implementation running forever and let each consuming team choose which output to use
Rewrite it in code directly on the main branch over a weekend and switch all consumers to the new implementation on Monday morning

stem: A marketing team needs campaign metrics refreshed every 15 minutes during a campaign week and daily otherwise. The source is an append-only event dataset. Which processing design balances freshness and cost?

choices.text: A streaming pipeline running permanently, since 15-minute freshness is only achievable with continuous processing
An incremental transform over new events, scheduled every 15 minutes in campaign weeks and daily otherwise
A daily batch at all times, with the marketing team told that intra-day metrics are not possible
Full batch every 15 minutes all year round, since campaign weeks cannot be predicted reliably enough to change the schedule

stem: An hourly transform is meant to add a new batch of rows to its output with APPEND transactions. Since a refactor, every run fails at commit with an error about modifying files that already exist in the dataset view. What is the cause and the fix?

choices.text: The schema of the output changed, and any schema change makes every later APPEND fail until the dataset is deleted and recreated
APPEND transactions can only be committed once per day, so the schedule must be changed from hourly to daily to stop the commit failures
The refactor writes the same output file name each run; an APPEND cannot modify existing files, so write a unique file per run
The output dataset has reached a storage quota, and old transactions must be deleted before any further APPEND can be committed

stem: A streaming pipeline is about to receive a 24-hour replay of historical messages after a source migration. What should the team prepare?

choices.text: A pause of all downstream consumers for a week until the replay is finished and the aggregates have been checked by hand
Nothing special, since a streaming pipeline simply processes whatever arrives in the order it arrives and the replay is just more messages
A temporary switch of the whole pipeline to batch mode for the replay, and a switch back to streaming afterwards once it is done
Capacity for the burst, idempotent processing against duplicates, event-time handling for old timestamps, and lag monitoring until it drains

stem: A data engineer is explaining incremental transforms to a colleague who is about to convert a nightly batch pipeline. Which statement about incremental transforms is correct?

choices.text: It never needs a full recompute once it has run successfully for the first time, because its state is kept forever from then on
It always processes only the single newest file in the input, regardless of how many transactions have arrived since its last successful run
It processes the input transactions added since its last successful run (typically APPENDs) and falls back when the increment is unsafe
It is only available in Pipeline Builder pipelines and cannot be implemented in Python or SQL code transforms in a repository

stem: A pipeline runs a heavy machine-learning feature computation nightly over the whole customer base, but only 3% of customers have any new activity each day. What should change?

choices.text: Switch the feature computation to a streaming pipeline so that features update in real time for every customer as events arrive
Make it incremental by key: recompute features only for customers with new activity and merge them in, with a periodic full recompute
Reduce the customer base processed each night to a random 3% sample, which matches the share of customers that actually changed
Nothing, since a nightly full batch is the standard approach for feature computation and the runtime is still acceptable

stem: A streaming job's checkpoint became corrupted after a storage incident, and the job cannot resume. What is the correct recovery?

choices.text: Reset the checkpoint to a known-good point or the earliest retained offset, replay idempotently, and reconcile the affected window
Delete the job and its output dataset and start again from an empty stream, accepting the permanent loss of all historical output
Restart the job from the latest available offset and ignore the gap between the corrupted checkpoint and now
Switch the pipeline to batch permanently, since the incident shows that streaming is unreliable for this data

stem: A dataset must retain a full history of every version of each record for audit, while consumers need only the current version. Which transaction and dataset design serves both?

choices.text: A spreadsheet export of each day's dataset kept in a shared folder, so that auditors can open the file for any past date
A single dataset in which DELETE transactions remove each old version as the new version of the record arrives
An append-only history dataset plus a derived current-state dataset built from it: audit reads history, consumers read current
A single dataset written as a SNAPSHOT on each run, holding only the current version of every record and nothing older

stem: A team is choosing between making a complex transform incremental (significant engineering, subtle state handling) or keeping it as a full nightly batch that currently takes 40 minutes on a 1 TB input growing 2% a month. What is a reasonable decision?

choices.text: Make it incremental immediately, since incremental processing is always superior to full batch regardless of the engineering cost
Reduce the input to the last month of data only so that the nightly batch stays fast forever as the dataset grows
Switch the transform to a streaming pipeline, which avoids the batch-versus-incremental question entirely
Keep the batch since it meets the window and incremental state is costly and risky, monitoring runtime with a revisit trigger

stem: A transform that ran in 20 minutes yesterday now runs in 3 hours. Job Comparison shows the same stages, but one stage's shuffle read grew from 2 GB to 400 GB. The input row count grew only 5%. What happened and what should be checked?

choices.text: A join's output multiplied because a duplicate key appeared in one input; check key uniqueness in the join inputs for today's data
The cluster was simply slower today because of other jobs; the build should be rerun at a quieter time when more resources are available
The dataset has too many small files, which the Linter would have flagged before the build ran
The transform's code was modified to add a new column, which explains the growth and requires no action beyond accepting it

stem: A pipeline's final dataset must be ready by 07:00 for a daily report. Its upstream sync lands between 03:00 and 05:30. The transforms take about 50 minutes. How should the schedule be designed to minimize risk of missing the deadline?

choices.text: A fixed 06:10 start, which leaves exactly enough time if the sync lands by 05:30 and the transforms take their usual 50 minutes
An input-update trigger that starts the pipeline when the sync lands, plus a freshness alert at 06:30 if the output is not yet built
A fixed 03:00 start every day, since starting the pipeline earlier is always safer when there is a hard morning deadline
A trigger at 07:00 that builds the report dataset exactly at the deadline so that the report contains the freshest possible data

stem: A build fails with "disk space exhausted" on executors during a wide aggregation. What is the likely cause and the right fix?

choices.text: The dataset is simply too large to process in Foundry in one job; split it across two separate pipelines that each handle half of the data
The output dataset's storage quota was exceeded during the write; request more storage quota from the platform administrators
A permission problem writing temporary files to executor disks; grant the build identity broader access to the storage layer
Shuffle spill exceeded local disk; reduce shuffle size by pre-aggregating or repartitioning, fix skew, or adjust resources, per Spark details

stem: A team needs an environment to test pipeline changes against production-like data without affecting production datasets or consumers. What should they use?

choices.text: A separate Foundry instance purchased solely for testing, with production data copied across to it periodically
A complete copy of all production datasets duplicated into a separate testing project every week by a scheduled job
Branches: develop on a branch whose builds read production inputs and write isolated branch outputs, with consumers unaffected until merge
Testing changes directly on the production datasets during an announced maintenance window when consumers are told not to rely on them

stem: An engineer is handling a failed build where the error message is unfamiliar. What is the most useful first evidence to gather?

choices.text: The opinions of colleagues who have worked on this pipeline about what usually goes wrong with it and how they fixed it before
The build logs and failing stage's error, the input transactions since the last good build, and the lineage of the failing dataset
The number of rows in the output dataset from the last successful build, as a baseline for what the failed build should have produced
The dataset's description field in the platform, which may mention known issues or contacts for the pipeline

stem: A pipeline has 30 datasets. Each dataset has its own schedule, and the team struggles to understand why some build out of order. What scheduling change helps?

choices.text: Setting all 30 schedules to exactly the same time so that the datasets build together and finish at roughly the same moment
Adding ten-minute offsets between consecutive datasets' schedules so that each one has time to finish before the next starts
Replacing per-dataset schedules with one pipeline schedule that builds the dependency graph in order, triggered by the root inputs
Removing all 30 schedules and having an engineer build everything manually in the correct order each morning

stem: A dataset's cost report shows its builds consuming far more compute than similar datasets. Spark details show 2,000 tasks for a 500 MB input and most tasks finishing in under a second. What is wrong?

choices.text: The executors must be faulty hardware if tasks finish that quickly, and they should be replaced by the platform team
Nothing; many short tasks indicate excellent parallelism and the cost report must be misattributing another pipeline's usage
The dataset is too small to be worth running on Spark at all and should be deleted from the pipeline to save the compute
Over-partitioning: far too many tiny tasks for a small input; coalesce or set an appropriate partition count so tasks do real work

stem: A pipeline intermittently fails on a transient network error reading from object storage, roughly one run in thirty. What is the proportionate operational response?

choices.text: Configure bounded automatic retries with backoff, alert only when retries are exhausted, and track the transient-failure rate for trends
Rewrite the pipeline so that it no longer reads from object storage at all, replacing the source with a database sync
Have the on-call engineer manually rerun every failed build as soon as the failure alert arrives, at any hour
Disable failure alerts for this pipeline entirely, since the failures are usually harmless and the next scheduled run fixes them

stem: A dataset feeds a pricing engine where a wrong currency code would cause incorrect charges. The currency column must always be one of 12 ISO codes. Which control is appropriate?

choices.text: A health check on the distribution of currency codes that alerts the owner when an unusual code appears in the published dataset
A build-blocking expectation that every currency value is in the allowed set of 12 codes, so any other value blocks publication
A note in the pipeline documentation listing the 12 allowed codes for consumers to verify
A transform that maps any unknown code to USD so the pricing engine never sees an unexpected value

stem: A freshness check on a dataset is green, but consumers report the data is weeks old. Investigation shows the pipeline rebuilds nightly and writes a transaction each time even though the source stopped delivering. What is the monitoring gap?

choices.text: Freshness was measured on transaction time, not content; add a content-freshness check (maximum event date) plus a check on the upstream source
There is no gap; a green freshness check means the data is fresh by definition and the consumers must be looking at the wrong dataset
The freshness threshold is too strict for a nightly pipeline and should be lengthened to several days to avoid false alarms
The check should be deleted since it gave a wrong answer and a check that can be wrong is worse than no check

stem: A pipeline's expectation on a `country` column fails when the source legitimately starts sending a new country code after the company expands. What process keeps expectations useful without blocking legitimate business change?

choices.text: Hard-code a very long list of every country code in the world into the expectation so that nothing new can ever appear
Remove allowed-value expectations from the pipeline entirely so that new country codes never cause build failures again
Let the on-call engineer edit the expectation's allowed list at night whenever a failure occurs, to keep the pipeline running
Keep the allowed set as governed reference data the business updates through review, with the expectation reading it

stem: A team wants to detect duplicate rows that appear occasionally after upstream retries. Duplicates are identical across all columns. Which check and placement are right?

choices.text: A health check that counts total rows in the curated dataset and alerts the owner whenever the count grows faster than the expected rate
A Linter rule configured to detect duplicate rows, since the Linter is the tool that checks pipeline data content
Idempotent deduplication in the transform, a uniqueness expectation on the curated output, and an upstream duplicate-rate check
A manual weekly query for duplicate rows run by an analyst, with any duplicates found reported to the pipeline team

stem: A data engineer is deciding, for each requirement on an orders dataset, whether to implement it as a build-blocking expectation or as a health check. Which requirement is best met by a health check?

choices.text: No order in the curated dataset may ever have a null customer id, since every order must belong to a known customer
The team should be told if the average order value shifts by more than 30% week over week, which may be a legitimate change
The primary key must be unique in the dataset backing the Order object type, since duplicate keys would corrupt objects
Order dates must never be in the future relative to the build date, since such rows indicate a source clock or entry error

stem: A data quality alert fires at 03:00 and the on-call engineer cannot tell from the message which dataset, which check or what threshold was breached. What should be improved?

choices.text: The alert should be downgraded to a weekly summary email so that it does not wake anyone up at night
Nothing; the on-call engineer can look through all of the team's datasets in the morning to find which one triggered the alert
The alert should be sent to more people across the organization so that someone will recognize which dataset it refers to
The alert content: dataset, check, observed value versus threshold, links to the dataset and lineage, and the runbook

stem: Which practice ensures that a newly created curated dataset has appropriate quality controls from day one?

choices.text: A definition-of-done: documented contract, key expectations, freshness and size checks, alert routing and runbook, before publishing
Copying the checks from a random existing dataset into the new one regardless of whether they fit its contract
Adding quality checks later, once the consuming teams have used the dataset for a while and complained about specific problems they found
Asking the consuming teams to write whatever checks they want on the dataset themselves after it is published

stem: A platform-wide review finds 1,200 health checks, a third of which have fired continuously for months without action. What should the data engineering team do?

choices.text: Delete all 1,200 health checks and start over from nothing, adding new checks one by one only when a specific need has been demonstrated
Lower every check's threshold across the platform until all 1,200 checks pass, so that the alert volume drops to zero
Triage each failing check as a real problem (fix) or a wrong assumption (re-baseline or retire), assign owners, forbid permanent red
Silence the failing third of the checks permanently so that the monitoring dashboard shows green for the platform
