stem: A dataset contains both personal data (names, emails) and non-sensitive operational columns. Two audiences need it: HR (everything) and operations (non-sensitive columns only). Which design uses the controls appropriately?

choices.text: Two copies of the full dataset in two projects, with operations asked not to use the personal columns in theirs
A single dataset with a PII marking, with operations staff granted the marking so that they can read the columns they need
A single unmarked dataset with a Workshop view for operations that hides the personal columns on screen
A PII-marked full dataset for HR and an unmarked derived dataset without the personal columns for operations, with lineage

stem: A pipeline references a dataset in another team's project. When the other team restructured their project into a new layout, the pipeline's input reference broke. How should cross-project dependencies be managed?

choices.text: Reference the other team's published curated outputs (not internal datasets) under an agreed contract, with moves coordinated via lineage
Copy the other team's dataset into your own project with a scheduled copy job so that their internal changes can never affect your pipeline
Ask the other team to commit in writing never to change their project structure or dataset locations again
Rebuild the other team's transformation logic inside your own pipeline from their raw sources so that you no longer depend on them

stem: A restricted view must show each sales rep their own accounts, their manager all accounts of their team, and the sales operations group everything. How should the policy be structured?

choices.text: Three separate restricted views, one per audience, each backed by its own filtered copy of the data maintained by the pipeline
A marking per sales team applied to the whole dataset, with each manager holding their own team's marking and sales operations holding all of them
One restricted view whose policy combines: row's rep equals the user, or row's team is one the user manages, or the user is in sales operations
A Workshop module that filters the account list by the logged-in user's name, with a toggle that managers can use to widen the view

stem: A dataset's owner reports that a contractor who left last month still appears to have access according to a report. What should the data engineer do?

choices.text: Nothing, since the contractor's account was disabled when they left and the remaining entitlements are therefore irrelevant
Verify with Check Access, remove the stale roles, group and marking memberships through process, and fix the offboarding gap
Delete the dataset and recreate it from scratch so that no historical grants to anyone can possibly remain on it
Rename and move the dataset to a different folder so that the contractor could not find it even if the account were re-enabled

stem: A project owner is trying to give a colleague read access to a dataset protected by a marking. Which action does NOT by itself grant the colleague the ability to read it?

choices.text: Adding the colleague to the marking's membership through the marking's own approval process so they hold it directly
Adding the colleague to an existing group that already holds the marking as part of its entitlements
Granting the colleague the Owner role on the project that contains the dataset, which is the highest project role available
Removing the marking from the dataset after a documented review concluding that the data is no longer sensitive

stem: A team wants external consultants to build pipelines in Foundry for three months without being able to see production customer data. How should their access be structured?

choices.text: No platform access at all, with the consultants writing transform code on their own laptops and employees uploading it into repositories
Full administrator access on the platform for the duration of the engagement so that the consultants are never blocked by permissions
Give the consultants Editor rights on the production projects and ask them in their contract to avoid opening any customer datasets
A development project with de-identified datasets where consultants have Editor rights and no production access; employees promote

stem: A build fails on a marked input although the build identity was recently added to the marking's membership. What should be checked?

choices.text: Whether the grant took effect, whether the build's actual identity was the one added, and whether another requirement applies, via Check Access
Whether the dataset's files are corrupted, since failures on marked datasets often indicate underlying file problems rather than access
Whether the transform's code needs an explicit marking annotation declaring that it is allowed to read the marked input
Whether the schedule ran too early in the day, since marking memberships granted during business hours only become active at midnight

stem: A team is deciding between a restricted view and separate per-region datasets to serve regional analysts. Which considerations favour the restricted view?

choices.text: Restricted views are always faster than querying separate datasets, so query performance alone decides the question in their favour
One pipeline and dataset, consistent logic, attribute-driven policies that follow user changes, simple lineage; with the all-rows caveat
Restricted views allow regional analysts to edit the underlying rows they can see, which separate per-region datasets do not allow
Restricted views do not require any permissions management at all once created, unlike datasets that need roles per project

stem: A company models Suppliers and Contracts. A contract can involve several suppliers (consortia), and a supplier has many contracts. Each supplier's share of a contract must be recorded. Which model is correct?

choices.text: A Contract object per supplier, duplicating the contract for each participant
A ContractParticipation object type keyed by contract and supplier, holding the share, linked many-to-one to both Contract and Supplier
A many-to-many link between Supplier and Contract with no properties, with the share stored as a list on the Contract object in the same order as the linked suppliers
A share property on Supplier, since each supplier has one share

stem: An object type's primary key is a composite of three source columns concatenated with a hyphen. Occasionally two different source rows produce the same key because one of the columns itself contains hyphens. What should change?

choices.text: Use the dataset row number as the primary key instead, which is guaranteed unique within any single build of the dataset
Drop the column that contains hyphens from the key so that only two clean columns remain and the delimiter scheme is unambiguous
Nothing; collisions are rare enough that the affected objects can be split and fixed by hand whenever someone notices a merge
Build the key unambiguously (an absent delimiter, escaping, or a hash of the typed components) and add a uniqueness expectation

stem: Applications need to filter Orders by the customer's country, which lives on the Customer object. Traversing the link for every filter is slow. What is the appropriate modeling response?

choices.text: Denormalize minimally: add a derived `customer_country` property to Order, computed in the pipeline and documented, keeping the link
Copy every Customer property onto each Order object so that applications never need to traverse a link for any customer attribute
Ask the application teams to stop offering a country filter on order lists, since the traversal cost makes it too expensive
Remove the Customer object type entirely and store all customer data only on the Orders that reference each customer

stem: A team must add a new required property to a live object type whose backing dataset currently lacks the column. Applications display the object type today. What sequence avoids breaking them?

choices.text: Add the property directly in production as optional for now and tell application teams to expect blank values until the pipeline catches up
Create a brand-new object type that includes the property and ask all application teams to switch their modules over to it
On a branch, produce the column with values for all rows, add the property to the object type, validate the applications, then merge together
Add the property as required in the Ontology first, then update the pipeline afterwards, accepting a short period in which objects fail validation

stem: A field "status" exists on five object types with slightly different allowed values and spellings in each. Applications want a consistent status filter. What should the data engineer propose?

choices.text: Leave each object type's status values as they are and let every application map the different spellings to a common set itself
Merge the five object types into a single generic object type so that the status property is automatically shared among them
Store the status as free text on every type and ask users to search carefully with wildcards when they filter by status
Define a shared property with a controlled status vocabulary, map each type's values to it in the pipelines, expose it on all five

stem: A data engineer is configuring the link between Invoice and Customer object types. Each Invoice belongs to exactly one Customer, and a Customer may have many Invoices. Which link cardinality is correct?

choices.text: Many-to-many between Invoice and Customer backed by a join dataset, since a customer has many invoices and that implies many-to-many
No link at all; a customer name property on each Invoice is enough for applications to show who the invoice belongs to
Many-to-one from Invoice to Customer, equivalently one-to-many from Customer to Invoice, backed by the customer id on the invoice
One-to-one from Invoice to Customer, since each invoice has exactly one customer and that is what one-to-one expresses

stem: An application needs "days until contract expiry" for every contract in a list. The value changes daily. Where should it come from?

choices.text: A value typed in by application users whenever they open a contract and notice that the number is out of date
A nightly materialized property if filtering is needed and a day's staleness is fine, or a value computed at display time if exactness matters
A property materialized nightly in the pipeline regardless of how it is used, which will be at most a day stale for every consumer
A manual update of the value by the contract team each morning before the application's users start their day

stem: After a backing dataset was rebuilt with a different sort order and a subtle change in how a key column was trimmed, 2% of objects lost their user edits. What happened and what should be done?

choices.text: The trimming change altered those rows' keys, re-identifying the objects and detaching edits; map old to new keys, re-attach, add tests
The lost edits were not important since only 2% of objects were affected, and users can re-enter them if they notice
The new sort order changed the keys of the affected rows, so sorting the dataset the old way in the transform will restore the edits
The Ontology randomly discards a small share of user edits during any large rebuild, and nothing in the pipeline can prevent that

stem: A data engineer is debugging a failing PySpark transform and wants help interpreting a long stack trace. Which capability is designed for this?

choices.text: AIP Assist, the platform helper, which fixes failing transforms automatically and redeploys them when given an error message
An embedding transform that compares the stack trace with previous traces in a dataset to find the most similar past failure
An LLM transform run over the stack trace stored as a single dataset row, producing an explanation column the engineer can read
A code assistant (Continue or AI FDE) in the development environment that reads the error and the code and suggests a diagnosis to review

stem: An LLM transform classifies supplier invoices by spend category. The finance team requires that every classification can be explained and traced. Which configuration satisfies this?

choices.text: An instruction in the prompt telling the model to be transparent about its reasoning when it assigns a category
Store only the category value per invoice, since storing explanations alongside it would roughly double the storage for the dataset
Structured output with category and reason, retention of prompt version, model and raw response per row, and a link to the source invoice
A monthly sample of ten classifications reviewed by the finance team, with the review notes stored in a shared document

stem: A team proposes running an LLM on every row of a 50 million row dataset nightly to compute a field that only 0.5% of rows (those with a non-empty free-text note) can actually have. What should the data engineer advise?

choices.text: Run it on all 50 million rows every night, since consistency of treatment across the dataset matters more than the compute cost
Filter deterministically to rows with a non-empty note that changed since the last run, run the LLM on those, null elsewhere
Run it on a random 10% sample of rows each night to save cost, accepting that most rows will never receive a value
Replace the LLM step with a deterministic rule that sets the field to "unknown" for all rows, removing the cost entirely

stem: A code assistant generated a SQL transform that uses a `SELECT *` from a wide input followed by downstream logic. Reviewers are concerned. Why, and what should change?

choices.text: `SELECT *` couples the output to the input's full schema, so new columns flow through; select columns explicitly and add a schema expectation
There is no concern; `SELECT *` is the simplest and most maintainable way to get all of the input's columns into the output
The transform should be converted to a Python transform, since SQL transforms cannot express column selection safely
The assistant should have used `SELECT ALL` instead of `SELECT *`, which is the recommended form for wide inputs

stem: An LLM transform occasionally returns responses that cannot be parsed into the expected structure. What should happen to those rows?

choices.text: Keep them with a failure status and raw response, exclude them from consumer-facing properties, count them, retry or review
They should cause the entire build to fail every time one occurs, so that no transaction with any parse failure is ever published
They should be filled with the most common category observed across the dataset so that the output has no gaps for consumers
They should be silently dropped from the output so that the dataset contains only well-formed rows and consumers see no errors

stem: A pipeline enriches customer records with an LLM-generated summary. Applications also offer a "regenerate summary now" button. How do the two relate?

choices.text: The button should trigger a full run of the enrichment pipeline so that every record's summary is regenerated at once
The pipeline should be replaced by the button entirely, since on-demand regeneration is always fresher than a scheduled batch
They are redundant ways of producing the same summary, so one of the two mechanisms should be removed to avoid confusion
The pipeline provides the baseline summary for every record; the button regenerates one record on demand via a versioned Action

stem: A team relies on an AI assistant to write expectations for new datasets. What should the engineer verify in the generated expectations?

choices.text: That they compile and run without errors on the current dataset, which is sufficient proof that the quality rules are correct
That the assistant added a comment above each expectation explaining its purpose, so reviewers can read the intent
That each reflects the real contract rather than column-name guesses, thresholds are justified, and severity matches consequence
That there are as many expectations as possible on the dataset, since more rules always mean better data quality

stem: Leadership asks the data engineering team to "put AI in every pipeline". What is a sound engineering response?

choices.text: Add AI only to pipelines that are already failing regularly, on the theory that they are the ones that most need improvement
Apply AI where it fits: rules stay deterministic, AI handles bounded interpretation of unstructured data under validation and checks
Refuse to use AI in any pipeline on the grounds that non-deterministic steps are too risky for governed data
Comply fully by adding an LLM step to every transform in every pipeline regardless of what the transform does or whether it needs one

stem: A team must ingest data from a mainframe system that exposes only fixed-width text files delivered once a day by file transfer. Which ingestion design is appropriate?

choices.text: A file sync that lands the files unchanged, then a transform that parses the fixed column positions from a documented layout, with expectations
A JDBC connection to the mainframe, since every enterprise system can be queried with SQL once the right driver is installed on the agent host
A manual process in which an operator opens each file in a spreadsheet, splits the columns by hand and uploads the result through the browser each morning
A streaming sync that reads each line of the daily file as it is written and emits it as a message to a streaming dataset for immediate processing

stem: An append sync keyed on an auto-incrementing id has started missing rows since the source migrated to a new database whose ids are no longer monotonic (a sharded id scheme). What should change?

choices.text: Run the sync twice per hour instead of once, since more frequent runs give each row more chances to be picked up before the watermark moves past it
Sort the source table by id before each run so that the ids become monotonic again from the sync's point of view
Keep the id-based append sync and accept the missing rows, since sharded ids are a source problem that the sync cannot be expected to work around
Switch the change signal to something monotonic (a commit timestamp or sequence number) or use CDC, and reconcile the rows missed

stem: A regulator requires that a monthly extract delivered to them contains exactly the agreed fields and is traceable to the source data used. How should the export be designed?

choices.text: A shared screen-sharing session in which the regulator views the dashboards and takes screenshots of the figures they need
Have an analyst assemble the extract by hand each month from several datasets and email it to the regulator with a note about where the data came from
A transform producing the extract with the agreed schema enforced by an expectation, lineage to the sources, and a governed, logged export
A direct export of the raw source datasets so the regulator has everything and can derive the fields they need themselves

stem: A sync has started taking four times longer than usual, though the record count is unchanged. Execution history shows the run spending most of its time waiting on the source. What should be investigated?

choices.text: The agent's installation, which should be reinstalled because slowdowns usually indicate a corrupted agent binary on the host
Source-side conditions: a dropped index on the queried column, increased source load, or a changed query plan
The downstream transforms, since a slow consumer can hold up the sync that feeds it
The dataset's expectations, since slow syncs are usually caused by expectation checks running on every row during ingestion

stem: A data engineer must choose between a direct connection and an agent for a cloud-hosted database that the platform can reach over a private network link. Which is the better default and why?

choices.text: Both at once, so that if one fails the other still delivers the data
An agent, because agents are always more secure than direct connections regardless of the network topology between platform and source
A direct connection, because the source is reachable and a direct connection avoids an agent host; agents are for unreachable sources
An agent, because cloud databases cannot be connected to directly from the platform

stem: A source table has a reliable `updated_at` column but rows are also physically deleted, and the consumers need deletions reflected within a day. CDC is not available. Which pattern fits?

choices.text: A streaming sync, since deletions can only be captured by continuous replication of the source
An update sync on `updated_at` only, since it captures every insert and update and those are the changes consumers care about most
A full snapshot every hour, since deletions make incremental patterns impossible
An update sync on `updated_at` for inserts and updates, plus a daily key-only snapshot (or a soft-delete flag) to detect deletions

stem: A virtual table over an external system suddenly returns an authentication error for all users, though nothing in Foundry was changed. What is the likely cause and the right fix?

choices.text: Every user's personal permissions on the external system were revoked at once, and each user must request access again individually
The connection's credentials or token expired or were rotated externally; update them in the governed source configuration and test
The external system no longer supports virtual tables, so the data must be copied into Foundry instead
The virtual table definition is corrupted and must be deleted and recreated from scratch by an administrator

stem: A team must design ingestion for a source that is known to be unreliable: late files, occasional duplicates, and sporadic schema drift. What design absorbs these without manual intervention?

choices.text: Layered: tolerant landing, parsing that absorbs additive drift and fails on breaking drift, key dedupe, realistic checks, quarantine
Asking the source team to fix their system's lateness, duplicates and drift before any ingestion is built on top of it
Skipping validation entirely so that the pipeline never fails, and letting consumers deal with duplicates and schema changes themselves
A strict sync that fails the moment anything deviates, so that the on-call engineer can review every problem by hand

stem: A dataset of product events has a JSON column containing nested attributes that differ by product category. The business wants a few common attributes as typed columns and the rest preserved. Which transformation approach is right?

choices.text: Dropping the JSON column entirely from the curated dataset because nested data cannot be handled properly in a tabular pipeline
Casting the whole JSON column to a string and asking consumers to parse whatever they need from it in their own tools
Exploding every nested key into its own column, producing thousands of mostly empty columns so that nothing is ever missed
Parsing the JSON, extracting the agreed common attributes into validated typed columns, keeping the original JSON for the long tail

stem: A Spark join between a 1 TB fact table and a 10 MB dimension table is slow because Spark shuffles the large table. What is the standard fix?

choices.text: Use a broadcast join so the small dimension is sent to every executor and the fact table joins in place without a shuffle
Convert the dimension table to a JSON string and parse it inside a UDF for every row of the fact table
Split the fact table into one dataset per day and join each one separately in a loop of 365 builds
Collect the fact table to the driver and loop over it in Python, since loops are easier to reason about than shuffles

stem: A transform's logic depends on a dozen business thresholds that change quarterly. The thresholds are currently hard-coded. What should the data engineer do?

choices.text: Keep them hard-coded and redeploy the transform every quarter when the business sends the new values
Move them into a governed reference dataset the business maintains through review, read at build time, with an expectation
Ask the business to stop changing the thresholds every quarter so that the transform's code can stay stable and tested
Put the thresholds in a comment at the top of the transform so they are easy to find when editing

stem: A pipeline must compute each customer's rolling 7-day spend ending on each day for the last year. Which transformation construct is appropriate?

choices.text: A Python loop over customers on the driver that slides a window through each customer's transactions one at a time
A self-join of the transactions table to itself for every pair of days within a week, which produces the rolling sums after filtering
A window function partitioned by customer, ordered by date, with a range frame over the preceding 7 days summing spend
A group-by on customer and week, which gives weekly totals that can be used as the rolling value

stem: A pipeline step must run a trained machine-learning model's inference library on each row, with the library's own Python dependencies. Which authoring choice fits?

choices.text: A notebook that an analyst runs weekly on their own machine and whose scored output is uploaded to the platform as a dataset
A Contour analysis that applies the model interactively whenever an analyst needs scores for a particular set of rows
Pipeline Builder, since model inference is a transformation like any other and can be configured visually
A code transform with the library and its dependencies declared, using batched inference, with tests on representative inputs

stem: A transform that aggregates sales by region started producing a new "null" region bucket containing 8% of revenue. Nothing in the transform changed. What is the right investigation and fix?

choices.text: Filter out the null-region rows in the transform so that the dashboard shows only the valid regions and no confusing bucket
Trace it upstream: the region join fails for new store codes or the source stopped populating region; fix it and add an expectation
Ask the dashboard owners to ignore the null bucket for now and revisit the issue when the team has more time next quarter
Rename the null bucket to "Other" in the output so that the dashboard looks tidy and the revenue is still counted somewhere

stem: A team runs twenty small transforms, each on Spark, each processing under 50 MB and taking three minutes, mostly startup. What should they consider?

choices.text: Combining all twenty into a single giant transform regardless of what they do
Increasing executor count on each transform so the three minutes become shorter
Moving these small transforms to a lightweight engine (or consolidating related ones), validated by comparing outputs on a branch
Nothing, since three minutes per transform is acceptable to consumers and Spark is the platform's standard engine for every transform

stem: A team wants every transform in a critical pipeline to be covered by automated checks before merge. Which combination gives meaningful coverage?

choices.text: Unit tests on transformation functions, a branch build compared against production, expectations on outputs, and required review
A rule that every transform must have a header comment explaining its purpose, enforced by a check that the comment is present
A monthly manual review of all transforms in the pipeline by the team lead, who reads through the code for anything suspicious
A single automated test that checks the whole pipeline compiles and runs without errors on a small sample before merge

stem: An insurance claims dataset receives new claims continuously, but the downstream fraud model only needs scores by the start of each business day. Claims occasionally receive corrections for up to 30 days. Which processing design fits?

choices.text: A streaming pipeline that scores every claim within seconds of arrival and never revisits it, since streaming is the most capable mode available
A full batch over all claims ever received every night, so that corrections are always reflected regardless of when they arrive
A lightweight single-node transform every hour over the complete claims history, since the logic is simple
A nightly incremental run over new and corrected claims (by key and update time), with a periodic recompute over the 30-day window

stem: A downstream dataset shows twice as many rows as expected after a run. The input is fed by an incremental file sync with APPEND, which ingests files not seen before, keyed by file path. The source re-delivered yesterday's export under a new, timestamped file name. What happened and what should be done?

choices.text: A new path counts as a new file, so the same content was appended twice; fix the re-delivery or naming, and deduplicate by key with a uniqueness expectation
The downstream transform has a bug that duplicates every row, unrelated to the input, and should be rewritten from scratch
Row duplication is normal after any APPEND, so every consumer should always deduplicate the data themselves
The platform automatically converted the APPEND into an UPDATE because the content matched, which is a platform defect to report to support

stem: A streaming pipeline computes per-customer session metrics with 30-minute inactivity windows. Events can arrive up to 10 minutes late. How should watermarks and windows be configured?

choices.text: No watermark, so that every late event is always included no matter when it arrives, at the cost of never finalizing any window
Processing-time windows, so that lateness does not matter because every event is assigned to a window by its arrival time at the pipeline
Event-time session windows with a 30-minute gap and about 10 minutes of allowed lateness, with events beyond that routed to a late-data path
A 10-second watermark, so that windows finalize quickly and late events are simply dropped

stem: Which of the following would NOT cause an incremental transform to fall back to a full recompute?

choices.text: An APPEND transaction on an input that added two new files since the last run
A SNAPSHOT transaction on an input that rewrote the whole dataset
A DELETE transaction on an input that removed a file the transform had already processed
An UPDATE transaction on one of its inputs that replaced a previously processed file

stem: A batch pipeline is asked to deliver results "as fresh as possible" by a stakeholder who cannot say what freshness they need. How should the data engineer proceed?

choices.text: Elicit the real requirement (what decision, how often), choose the cheapest mode that meets it, document and monitor it
Run the full batch every minute to be safe, so that whatever freshness the stakeholder has in mind is certainly met
Keep the current nightly batch exactly as it is and tell the stakeholder that the pipeline's freshness cannot be changed
Build a streaming pipeline immediately, since "as fresh as possible" means real time

stem: A streaming pipeline's lag grows steadily every afternoon and recovers overnight. What does this pattern indicate and what should be done?

choices.text: The pipeline should be switched to batch mode during the afternoon peak and back to streaming when the input rate drops again
The source system is broken in the afternoons and should be restarted automatically every day at 14:00 to clear the problem
Lag growth during busy hours is normal for any streaming pipeline and requires no action as long as it recovers by the next morning
Throughput is below the afternoon input rate: scale processing or reduce per-event cost, and set a lag alert threshold

stem: A dataset must be rebuilt from scratch monthly to apply a corrected definition, but consumers must never see an empty or partial dataset during the rebuild. Which transaction approach achieves this?

choices.text: Rebuilding into the same dataset file by file with UPDATE transactions as each recomputed file completes over the course of the run
Deleting all of the existing files first and then appending the recomputed files over several hours while consumers wait for the rebuild
Writing the full recomputed output as one SNAPSHOT transaction, which atomically replaces the previous view only when complete
Appending the recomputed files on top of the old ones and asking every consumer to filter by build date to get the corrected version

stem: A team wants an incremental transform to be safe against duplicate processing if a run is retried after a partial failure. Which design principle must the transform follow?

choices.text: Each run must write its output to a brand-new dataset so that any duplicates from a retry are isolated in a separate place
Idempotency: processing an increment once or several times must yield the same output (keyed merges or deduplication)
Retries must be disabled entirely in the schedule so that duplicate processing of any increment becomes impossible
Processing must be made as fast as possible so that failures and therefore retries become rare enough not to matter

stem: A transform's output row count dropped by 40% overnight with no code change, and the build succeeded. Which evidence sequence finds the cause fastest?

choices.text: Asking consumers whether they noticed the difference, since their feedback indicates which rows disappeared
Comparing input transactions since the last good build (counts, schema), then walking lineage to the first dataset whose count dropped
Rewriting the transform from scratch and comparing the new version's output with the old one to see whether the counts come back
Increasing the transform's executor memory, since dropped rows are usually caused by memory pressure during the join stage

stem: Three independent source syncs feed one curated dataset, and each source lands at a different, unpredictable time. The business wants the curated dataset refreshed whenever any one source updates, not only when all three have. How should the schedule be configured?

choices.text: An event-based schedule triggered by an update to any of the three inputs, with a minimum interval to avoid rapid repeated builds
Three separate copies of the curated dataset, one per source, each rebuilt when its own source lands
A schedule every five minutes that force-builds the curated dataset regardless of input changes
A single daily schedule at midnight that builds the curated dataset once, since partial refreshes are confusing for consumers

stem: A build fails with a message that the output dataset's schema is incompatible with the existing dataset (a column type changed). The change was intentional. What is the correct release step?

choices.text: Disabling schema checks on the dataset permanently so that any future type change goes through
Casting the column back to its old type in the transform so that the build passes, abandoning the intended change for now
Deleting the output dataset and letting the build recreate it, losing history and breaking consumers
Releasing it deliberately: notify consumers via lineage, choose a compatible rollout (new column or schema snapshot), validate on a branch

stem: A pipeline's compute cost has grown 300% over a year while its data grew 20%. Which review approach finds the waste?

choices.text: Deleting the oldest half of the datasets, since old datasets are the most likely to be wasteful
Switching every transform in the pipeline to the smallest executor configuration available and seeing which ones fail under the new limits
Reviewing build frequency against consumption, Spark details for partitioning, skew and full recomputes, and orphaned pipelines, fixing by impact
Asking the platform team to lower the price of compute

stem: A transform fails intermittently with an error indicating that an input file was not found, although the file exists when the engineer checks afterwards. What is the likely cause and remedy?

choices.text: The platform randomly hides files from builds under load; the only remedy is to retry the build until the file happens to appear
The read overlaps an in-progress upstream write or compaction; trigger the transform on the upstream's commit instead of a timer
The transform's code references the file by an incorrect name on some days of the week because of a date-formatting bug in the path
The file is too large and sometimes fails to load within the read timeout, which the platform reports as a file-not-found error

stem: A pipeline currently rebuilds a 500 GB curated dataset hourly to serve a dashboard that most users open between 08:00 and 18:00. Overnight builds are never looked at. What scheduling change is reasonable?

choices.text: Hourly builds during business hours and a single overnight build (or event-triggered builds), serving users when they actually look
Stopping all scheduled builds and asking users to request a manual refresh from the team whenever they need current data
Keeping hourly builds around the clock exactly as now, since a consistent cadence matters more than the compute cost of overnight builds
Building every 15 minutes during business hours to be extra fresh

stem: An engineer must hand over a pipeline to another team. What should the handover include so the new team can operate it?

choices.text: A copy of the pipeline's datasets placed in the new team's project, so that they have the data they need from day one
A verbal walkthrough over a couple of meetings and a copy of the engineer's personal notes about the pipeline's quirks
Documented contracts, schedule and triggers, checks with rationale, rerouted alerts, runbooks, consumer list, and an access review
Just the repository link and a short message, since well-written transform code explains itself to any competent engineer

stem: A build runs successfully but takes four hours, and Spark details show 95% of the time in a single final stage writing output with one task. What is the cause and fix?

choices.text: The transform has too many small input files to read efficiently; compact the input datasets so the build reads fewer, larger files
The build identity lacks write permissions on the output and the platform is silently retrying the write for hours before giving up
The output dataset's underlying storage is slow for large writes; request faster storage from the platform team for this dataset
The output is written through a single partition (after a coalesce(1) or global sort); repartition before writing and confirm

stem: A dataset backs an object type whose primary key must be unique, but the team also wants to know when the share of rows with a missing optional "phone" field rises above 20%, which may indicate a source change but is not an error. Which configuration fits both?

choices.text: Neither, since monitoring optional fields is not worth the effort
A build-blocking uniqueness expectation on the key, and a health check on the phone null rate with an alert at 20%
Build-blocking expectations for both conditions, since any deviation from expected data should stop the pipeline until someone reviews it
Health checks for both conditions, since alerts are less disruptive than build failures

stem: A health check on a dataset's size has fired because the dataset grew 3× overnight. The build succeeded. What should the engineer check first?

choices.text: Whether the health check's growth threshold is simply too tight for this dataset and should be tripled so it stops firing
Whether the project's storage quota is about to run out, since dataset growth alerts are primarily there to warn about capacity
Whether a join multiplied rows, an upstream delivered a duplicate load, or an incremental transform re-appended, via keys and inputs
Whether any consumers have complained about the dataset, since a size alert that nobody has noticed downstream is probably not real

stem: A new source sometimes delivers a file with an entirely wrong schema (a different report accidentally dropped into the folder). The team wants the pipeline to keep publishing good data while isolating the bad file. What should be configured?

choices.text: Per-file schema validation at parse time that routes non-conforming files to quarantine with an alert while conforming files continue
Deleting any file that fails to parse immediately, so that the pipeline never stalls and the folder stays clean
A build-blocking expectation on the parsed dataset so that the entire build fails and nothing publishes whenever a wrong file appears
Manual inspection of every incoming file by an engineer before it is moved into the folder the pipeline reads from

stem: Which health-check design detects that a daily dataset was built with yesterday's input again (the source delivered nothing new but the build ran)?

choices.text: A schema check on the dataset, since reprocessing yesterday's input a second time changes the schema of the output
A row-count check with a tight threshold, since reprocessed data always produces a noticeably different row count
A build-status check on the dataset, since the build would fail or be skipped automatically when the input is unchanged
A content-freshness check on the maximum event date, plus a freshness check on the upstream source dataset

stem: A data engineer is explaining to a new colleague how expectations and health checks should be used on a critical curated dataset. Which statement about their relationship is accurate?

choices.text: Health checks are the newer replacement for expectations and should be used instead of them on any dataset created from now on
Expectations and health checks are mutually exclusive mechanisms, so a dataset should be configured with one or the other but never both
They complement each other: expectations block invalid transactions at build time, health checks detect drift over time; use both
Expectations only apply to streaming datasets while health checks only apply to batch datasets, so the dataset's mode decides

stem: Consumers report that a dataset's `amount` column has been in cents since last week instead of dollars. No check fired. Which checks would have caught it, and what should be added?

choices.text: Statistical content checks on the column (median band, ratio to a related column) and reconciliation against a source total
A build-status check on the dataset, since a unit change in a numeric column causes the build to fail with a type error
A null-rate check on the amount column, since a unit change in the source usually produces null values during conversion
A schema check on the dataset, since the column's type effectively changed from a dollar amount to a cent amount

stem: An expectation requires that `country` be one of 40 codes. The business adds a 41st country, and the build fails on the first rows from it. Which process should be in place so this does not block the business?

choices.text: Changing the expectation to a non-blocking warning so that any country value passes and the build never fails on it
Removing the allowed-values expectation entirely, since the list of countries changes over time and the check keeps causing failures
Having the on-call engineer edit the expectation's hard-coded list whenever the build fails on a new country code
An expansion process where the business updates the governed country reference the expectation reads before go-live, so the new code passes

stem: A team wants a weekly data-quality report for a domain's datasets that is useful to both engineers and business owners. What should it contain?

choices.text: A screenshot of the monitoring dashboard taken on Friday afternoon and attached to an email to the domain owners
Per dataset: expectation history, check status and incidents, freshness against SLA, content metrics, owned open issues, layered by audience
A raw dump of every check result from the week in a single table, so that nothing is left out of the report
Only a count of alerts fired during the week, since that is the simplest metric to compute and the easiest for everyone to read

stem: A dataset must be readable by the whole company except for a single highly sensitive column that only the legal team may see. Which design achieves this cleanly?

choices.text: Encrypting the sensitive column's values with a personal key that only a few legal staff know, inside the same dataset
A curated dataset without the column for the company, plus a separate keyed dataset holding the column under a legal marking
Applying a legal marking to the entire dataset so that only the legal team can open it, and asking everyone else to request the data from legal
Leaving the dataset unmarked and relying on a Workshop module to hide the sensitive column from non-legal users

stem: A data engineer discovers that a project's Owner role was granted to a broad "all-employees" group years ago, so anyone can delete datasets in it. What is the right remediation?

choices.text: Replacing the broad Owner grant with least-privilege roles (Viewer, Editor, a small Owner group), auditing changes, adding reviews
Leaving the grant as it is, since nobody has deleted anything in the project so far and changing roles might disrupt users
Deleting the whole project and recreating it from scratch with the right permissions, then re-adding the datasets to it
Renaming the project to something obscure so that fewer of the employees in the group ever find it in search

stem: A restricted view policy must grant rows based on a user attribute (region) that is stored in an HR system, not in the platform. How should this be set up?

choices.text: Hard-coding each user's region directly into the restricted view's policy, updated by hand whenever someone moves to a new region
Asking each user to declare their own region in a prompt when they open the dataset, and filtering rows on what they declared
Granting every user access to every region's rows, which avoids the mapping problem by removing the restriction altogether
Syncing the user-to-region mapping from HR into a governed dataset or user attributes the policy references, so HR changes flow through

stem: A dataset's lineage shows it is derived from a marked source, but the dataset itself carries no marking and is readable by a broad audience. What should the data engineer do?

choices.text: Delete the dataset to be safe
Investigate: if sensitive content propagated, apply the marking and assess exposure; if de-identified, document the review
Nothing, since the marking only applies to the source dataset
Add a note in the dataset's description warning readers that the data may be sensitive and should be handled carefully

stem: A data engineer is onboarding a partner company's analysts and needs to explain why they cannot see internal projects. Which statement correctly describes organizations in the access model?

choices.text: Organizations are simply another name for projects, so a partner's analysts need only be added to the right project to see it
Organizations replace markings for sensitive data, so a dataset in the right organization needs no marking to be protected
Organizations are optional labels used for reporting with no effect on access, since only markings and project roles decide what a user can see
Organizations partition the platform: cross-organization visibility is restricted by default, and markings and roles apply within

stem: Two business units must share a curated reference dataset while keeping all their other data separate. How should this be structured?

choices.text: Placing the shared reference dataset in a dedicated shared project readable by both units and referenced from their own projects
Giving each unit full access to the other's projects so the reference data is visible
Merging both business units' projects into a single project so that everything is visible to everyone and nothing needs sharing
Duplicating the reference dataset into each unit's project and having the two teams keep the copies in sync by hand whenever it changes

stem: An Ontology object type is readable by a user, but one of its link types to another object type returns nothing for them while colleagues can traverse it. What is the likely cause?

choices.text: The link type's configuration is broken for this user and must be deleted and recreated by the Ontology owner
The user lacks access to the linked object type's backing data (a marking, role or view on that side); use Check Access there
The user's browser is caching an old version of the Ontology from before the link type was created, and a hard refresh will fix it
Links are randomly hidden from some users for performance reasons when the linked object type is large

stem: A team debates whether to implement row-level security with a restricted view or by baking the filter into a Workshop module's queries. Which argument correctly favours the restricted view?

choices.text: Workshop queries with filters are slower than restricted views, so query performance alone decides the question in favour of the view
Workshop modules cannot filter data at all
A restricted view enforces the restriction at the data layer for every access path; a module filter protects one module only
Restricted views are easier and quicker for a data engineer to build than configuring filters inside a Workshop module

stem: A company has Vehicles and Drivers. A driver can be assigned to several vehicles over time, a vehicle has many drivers over time, and at any moment a vehicle has at most one current driver. Which model captures both history and the current assignment efficiently?

choices.text: A list of driver names stored on each Vehicle object in chronological order, with the last entry treated as the current driver
A current_driver property on Vehicle only, overwritten on every change, since the assignment history is not usually needed by anyone
An Assignment object type with vehicle, driver, start and end, linked to both, plus a derived current-driver link on Vehicle
A single many-to-many link between Vehicle and Driver with no properties, since that expresses that drivers and vehicles are related in both directions

stem: An Order object type's primary key comes from a source column that is unique per source system, but orders now arrive from two source systems whose ids overlap. What should the key become?

choices.text: A namespaced key combining the source system and the source order id, with a uniqueness expectation and a migration mapping existing objects
The order's row number in the combined dataset after the two sources are unioned, which is unique within each build
A random UUID generated at build time for every row, which guarantees that no two orders ever share a primary key
The same source column as before, accepting that overlapping ids will occasionally merge orders from the two systems into one object

stem: Two teams want to model "Customer" independently for their own applications, with different properties and keys. What should the data engineer recommend?

choices.text: Model customers as free-text name and address fields on each team's Order objects instead of creating any Customer object type
Let each team create its own Customer object type with its own key and properties, since independence avoids coordination costs
Pick one team's model as the only Customer object type and force the other team to abandon the properties their application needs
One shared Customer object type with a governed key and core properties, extended by team-specific properties or linked satellite types

stem: A backing dataset's refresh must change from nightly to hourly for an object type used by a live operations app. What should be verified before making the change?

choices.text: That all users of the app have been told by email to refresh their browsers every hour so that they see the latest data
That hourly builds and indexing keep up, that keys stay stable between builds, that user edits are preserved, and that the app handles refreshes, on a branch
Nothing in particular; a faster refresh is always better and the operations app will simply show newer data every hour
That the operations app has been completely rewritten to expect hourly data instead of nightly data before the change is made

stem: An application must show, for each Product, its current price and the full price history. Prices change weekly. How should this be modeled?

choices.text: A single price property on Product overwritten weekly, with the history reconstructed from the dataset's transactions whenever anyone needs it
A PriceVersion object type (product, price, effective range) linked to Product, plus a derived current_price property on Product
A separate Product object created for every price change, so that each object carries exactly one price and its date
A list of all historical prices stored as an array property on Product, with the most recent one at the end of the list

stem: Which key choice is most likely to remain stable across rebuilds, source migrations and corrections?

choices.text: A business identifier assigned once by the system of record, or a deterministic hash of only the columns that identify the entity
The timestamp of the build concatenated with a per-build counter, which is unique across all builds and all datasets
The row's position in the dataset, which is guaranteed unique within a build and requires no knowledge of the business
A hash of all columns in the row, so that any change to the row produces a new key and nothing is ever silently overwritten

stem: A quality score for each Supplier is computed from a complex model over the supplier's delivery history. Procurement wants to filter suppliers by score in lists and also wants an explanation of the score on demand. Where does each part go?

choices.text: Both north: compute the score and the explanation with a function at the moment the user opens a supplier in the application
Neither; procurement should compute the scores and write the explanations in a spreadsheet that they maintain themselves
Both south, pre-generating a text explanation for every supplier nightly in the pipeline alongside the score
The score south as a materialized property for filtering, and the explanation north, generated on demand from the stored components

stem: After a backing dataset switched to an incremental build, some objects now show properties from older rows (the latest value is not reflected). What is the likely modeling or pipeline issue?

choices.text: Incremental builds cannot back object types at all, so the backing dataset must return to a full nightly batch immediately
The object type's primary key must be changed to a different column, since the current key no longer works with incremental data
The incremental output has multiple rows per key because corrections were appended, not merged; produce one current row per key and add a uniqueness expectation
The Ontology ignores datasets built incrementally and keeps serving the last full-batch version until a full build runs again

stem: A data engineer wants to quickly understand an unfamiliar pipeline with forty transforms before modifying it. Which AI capability helps most, and how should its output be treated?

choices.text: An LLM transform run over the repository's source files, producing a dataset of explanations that is then trusted as the pipeline's documentation
A code assistant that summarizes the transforms, their inputs, outputs and likely intent, verified against lineage and the code before changes
AIP Assist, which will automatically refactor the forty transforms into a cleaner structure that is easier to understand before the change
An embedding transform over the code files so that transforms similar to the one being modified can be found by semantic search

stem: An LLM transform must produce a numeric "urgency" from 1 to 5 for support tickets, and downstream logic sorts by it. The model sometimes returns 0, 6 or "high". What configuration prevents bad values from reaching the sort?

choices.text: A range-constrained integer in the schema, validation rejecting values outside 1 to 5, a status column for rejects, and a range expectation
Asking the model politely in the prompt to stay between 1 and 5 and to never answer with words, which it usually respects
Sorting the tickets by the raw text of the model's answer so that unusual values such as "high" simply sort to the end of the list
Casting whatever the model returns to an integer in the transform and defaulting any cast failure to a middle value of 3

stem: A company wants customer-facing chat to answer questions about order status using an LLM. The data engineering team is asked what they own in this design. Which answer reflects the role boundary?

choices.text: Nothing at all, since AI projects are outside data engineering and the AI team can read whatever data it needs directly
Everything in the design, including the chat agent's prompts, tools and conversation behaviour, since the data engineering team knows the data best
The curated, timely order data in the Ontology (object types, links, freshness, quality) and pipeline-layer AI enrichment; not the agent
Only the raw ingestion of order data from the source systems; everything after that, including the Ontology model, belongs to the AI team

stem: A code assistant generated a transform whose unit tests all pass, but the branch build shows the output has 12% fewer rows than the production version. What should the engineer conclude?

choices.text: A 12% difference in row count is within the normal variation that any transform shows from build to build and needs no investigation
The branch build must be broken in some way and should be ignored, since the unit tests are the authoritative check for correctness
The passing tests prove the generated code is correct, so the production version must have been wrong all along and can be replaced
The tests cover only the cases the assistant imagined; the branch comparison reveals a real difference to investigate before merge

stem: An LLM transform is used to extract a product category from descriptions, and the category feeds a restricted view policy (some categories are confidential). What additional care applies?

choices.text: Lowering the confidence threshold so that more rows receive a category and fewer end up unclassified in the view's policy
Stricter validation (enumeration, confidence thresholds, review of uncertain rows), monitoring, and a documented decision with a safe default
None; the category is just another column in the dataset and the restricted view treats it like any other value
Using the model's output directly in the restricted view policy without any validation, since validation would slow the pipeline

stem: A data engineering team is listing which AI-related work items in a new programme fall within their role. Which is the best example of pipeline-layer AI that a data engineer would own?

choices.text: The model-selection decision for a customer-facing assistant, weighing capability, latency and cost across the catalog
A chat interface embedded in the executive dashboards that lets executives explore the figures conversationally
An agent in Agent Studio that answers analysts' ad hoc questions about the sales data in natural language with retrieval and tools
A nightly LLM transform normalizing free-text supplier names into canonical identifiers, validated against the reference, feeding Supplier

stem: An assistant offers to generate the entire data model (object types, links, keys) for a new domain from a description. How should the data engineer use this?

choices.text: Publish the generated model and fix any modeling problems later as application users report them in production
Accept the generated model as it is and publish the object types immediately, since it was produced quickly and looks reasonable
Treat it as a draft: verify keys and cardinalities against the real data and business needs, correct the assumptions, validate on a branch first
Reject the generated model entirely and start from a blank page, since AI assistants cannot contribute anything useful to data modeling

stem: A team wants to measure whether their use of AI assistants for pipeline development is actually improving outcomes. What should they track?

choices.text: Delivery and quality outcomes: lead time, defects caught in validation and production, review findings, incidents, before and after
How much the engineers say they like working with the assistant in a monthly satisfaction survey run by the team lead
The number of prompts each engineer sends to the assistant per week, as a measure of how much the team has adopted the tool
Nothing, since AI assistants are obviously beneficial for development work and measuring it would waste the time it saves

stem: A partner delivers data by pushing JSON events to an HTTPS endpoint whenever records change, at a rate of a few hundred events per minute. The business wants the data available within a couple of minutes. Which ingestion pattern fits?

choices.text: A manual process in which an analyst downloads the partner's events each morning from a web portal and uploads them as a spreadsheet
A push-based streaming ingestion endpoint receiving the events, with a payload schema and a transform to current state
A nightly file sync that asks the partner to write the day's events into a single file in a bucket, so that the data arrives in one daily batch
A JDBC sync against the partner's database, since every partner exposes a database that can be queried directly over the internet

stem: A snapshot sync of a large table takes six hours and occasionally overlaps with the next run. The table has a reliable `updated_at` column and deletions are rare and soft-flagged. What should change?

choices.text: Increase the agent host's memory so that the snapshot finishes faster, since snapshot duration depends mostly on agent resources
Keep the snapshot and run it less often, accepting that the dataset is stale for most of the week between runs
An update sync on `updated_at` with a lookback, the soft-delete flag carrying deletions, and periodic reconciliation
Split the table into ten copies at the source and snapshot each one separately in parallel every night

stem: An external auditor needs read-only, time-limited access to a curated dataset. The organization prefers not to create platform accounts for auditors. What is the appropriate approach?

choices.text: Produce the agreed extract as a dataset and deliver it through a governed, logged export to an approved destination
Email the full curated dataset to the auditor's personal address as a compressed attachment
Share the platform credentials of an internal employee with the auditor for the duration of the audit, then reset the password
Make the curated dataset publicly accessible on the internet for the duration of the audit

stem: A file sync reports success, but downstream parsing fails because some landed files are truncated. The source writes large files slowly over several minutes. What is the likely cause and fix?

choices.text: The parsing transform is buggy and should be rewritten to tolerate truncated JSON by guessing the missing closing characters
The bucket is losing data and the storage provider should be changed
The agent is corrupting files in transit and should be reinstalled on a new host
The sync reads files still being written; use a completion signal (marker file, rename after write, minimum age)

stem: A team is deciding how to bring in data from a SaaS tool that offers both a REST API and a nightly CSV export to a bucket. The business needs daily freshness and the full history. Which statement best guides the choice?

choices.text: Either can work; choose by completeness, rate limits, schema stability and operational cost for the requirement
The REST API is always the better choice because APIs are more modern than files, regardless of limits or completeness
Both should be ingested in parallel into the same dataset to be safe
The CSV export is always worse because files cannot be governed in the platform

stem: A source table with 2 billion rows needs to be replicated with deletions and updates reflected within minutes, and the database supports change data capture. Which design fits?

choices.text: An hourly full snapshot of all 2 billion rows, since full snapshots are the only pattern that always captures deletions correctly
An append sync on the primary key, since higher keys always mean newer rows
An initial bulk load plus a CDC sync of the change log, with a keyed transform applying all changes to current state
A daily export to CSV from the database followed by a file sync

stem: An object type is backed by a virtual table over an external warehouse. Users see fewer objects than the warehouse table contains, and the difference depends on the user. The warehouse connection uses one service credential and nothing changed in the warehouse. What should be investigated first?

choices.text: Whether those users' browsers are caching an older copy of the objects from before the latest sync of the table
Foundry-side controls on the object type (object security policies) for those users, using Check Access, since the source sees one credential
Whether the virtual table should be replaced with a full copy so that every user sees the same row count
Whether the warehouse is applying each Foundry user's own warehouse permissions, since virtual tables pass every user's identity to the source

stem: Leadership wants every new data source onboarded within a week. The data engineering team wants a repeatable process that does not sacrifice quality. What should the onboarding standard include?

choices.text: A rule that every source must be streaming so that freshness is always maximal
A standard template: owner and credentials, landing dataset, documented keys, expectations, health checks, alerts and a runbook
Only the sync itself, with quality checks, alerts and documentation added later whenever consumers find problems in the data
A separate custom design for each source by whichever engineer is free that week

stem: Two datasets must be combined: one lists every customer, the other lists only customers who placed orders this month with their totals. The output must include all customers, with a zero total for those without orders. Which join and handling are correct?

choices.text: A left join from customers to the totals on customer id, with the total coalesced to zero when unmatched
A right join from customers to the totals, which keeps every customer whether or not they ordered
An inner join on customer id, since only matched customers have meaningful totals for the month
A cross join followed by a filter on matching ids, which produces the same result as any other join

stem: A Spark transform runs fine but its output dataset consists of 20,000 tiny files, which slows every downstream read. What should the engineer change?

choices.text: Increase the executor count on the downstream transforms so that they can open the 20,000 files faster
Convert the output to CSV so that the files are easier to read for any tool that needs them
Repartition the output to a sensible partition count before writing, then confirm file count and read time
Ask downstream consumers to read the files in smaller batches so that the number of files matters less to them

stem: A pipeline produces a dataset used for financial reporting. The finance team wants to know, for any month, exactly which version of the transformation logic produced the numbers. What should the engineering practice provide?

choices.text: A spreadsheet maintained by hand by the team lead that lists the dates on which the transform code was changed and by whom
A promise from the engineer that the logic has not changed since the last audit
A screenshot of the transform code taken at each month end
Reviewed, versioned code, builds tied to the commit that produced each transaction, and lineage to inputs

stem: A transform that computes average order value per region produces a value that is far too low for one region. Investigation shows many orders in that region have a null amount. How should the computation handle this?

choices.text: Treat null amounts as zero in the average, since a missing value most likely means the order was free of charge
Agree null semantics with the business, usually excluding nulls and reporting their count, and monitor the null rate
Drop the region from the output until the nulls disappear on their own
Replace null amounts with the global average so the region's figure looks normal

stem: An analyst-friendly Pipeline Builder pipeline has grown to 150 nodes with deeply nested logic, and changes now take days to review. What is a sensible next step?

choices.text: Rewrite the whole pipeline in code over a weekend and replace the original on Monday without comparing the outputs
Refactor into stages with intermediate datasets and contracts, moving complex reusable logic into tested code
Keep adding nodes to the same pipeline, since visual pipelines can grow without limit
Freeze the pipeline and prohibit further changes

stem: A transform joins a 2 TB events table to a 300 GB sessions table on session id. Both are large. Which optimization is appropriate when the join is the bottleneck?

choices.text: Convert both tables to CSV before joining to make them easier to read
Broadcast the 300 GB sessions table to every executor so that the much larger events table never needs to be shuffled
Collect the sessions table to the driver and look up sessions in a Python dictionary
Prune both sides early, co-partition or bucket them on session id, and check for skew in Spark details

stem: Which practice best prevents a transform change from silently altering a published dataset's output?

choices.text: A branch build compared with production output (counts, keys, metrics), plus expectations and unit tests
Merging quickly and checking the dashboard the next morning
Running the transform locally on ten handwritten rows
Reading the code diff carefully during review, which is enough for an experienced reviewer to see any change in the output

stem: A team must implement a transformation that standardizes company names across several sources (removing suffixes like "Inc." or "GmbH", fixing case, handling known aliases). Which implementation is most maintainable?

choices.text: A manual cleaning step in a spreadsheet each week before the data is uploaded
A single long expression in one visual node with dozens of nested replace calls written inline for every rule and alias
A tested code function with ordered rules and a governed alias reference dataset the business can update
An LLM call for every name on every run with no validation or caching

stem: A logistics company needs vehicle positions on an operations map within seconds, and also a daily report of distance driven per vehicle. Positions arrive as a continuous stream of GPS events. Which processing design fits both needs?

choices.text: A lightweight single-node transform run every minute over the complete history of GPS events for every vehicle in the fleet
A streaming pipeline for latest positions on the map, plus a daily batch over the persisted events for distances
A nightly batch over all GPS events that updates both the operations map and the daily distance report once per day at midnight
A streaming pipeline that also recomputes every vehicle's lifetime distance from scratch on every incoming GPS event

stem: A dataset is corrected by replacing a few hundred rows in one file each week. Downstream consumers use incremental transforms. Which transaction approach minimizes downstream impact?

choices.text: Edit the file in place outside the platform and hope the transaction history does not notice the change
Rewrite the entire dataset as a SNAPSHOT every week, since that guarantees the correction is applied everywhere at once
Delete the dataset and recreate it each week so that consumers always see a clean copy with every correction applied
Design the corrections as appended correction records keyed to the original rows, merged downstream by key

stem: A streaming aggregation's state size grows without bound over weeks, eventually slowing the job. The aggregation counts events per user per day. What is the likely cause and fix?

choices.text: The streaming engine leaks memory, so the job should be restarted every night to clear the state manually
The stream simply has more users every week, so unbounded state growth is expected and only more memory can address it
State for past days is never expired; add a time-to-live or watermark-based cleanup so finished days are emitted and dropped
The checkpoint location is too small, so it should be moved to a larger storage location without any other change

stem: An incremental transform aggregates daily sales. A new requirement adds a column computed from a reference table that changes monthly. How should the transform handle a monthly reference change?

choices.text: Treat a reference change as a controlled recompute: detect the new version and rerun the affected range
Copy the reference values into every sales row at the source so that the reference table is never needed by the pipeline
Hard-code the current reference values into the transform and update the code manually each month after the change
Ignore the reference change, since incremental transforms only process new sales rows and cannot use reference tables at all

stem: Which situation most clearly calls for streaming rather than frequent incremental batch?

choices.text: Fraud detection on card transactions where a decision must be made within a second, before the purchase completes
A monthly regulatory filing that is prepared from a complete and audited set of the previous month's ledger entries
A finance report reviewed every morning that needs data complete up to midnight of the previous day
A weekly marketing dashboard refreshed on Monday mornings for the leadership meeting at nine o'clock

stem: Consumers of a dataset report that rows they saw yesterday have disappeared today, although the source still has them. Transaction history shows yesterday's APPEND followed by today's SNAPSHOT containing only today's rows. What happened?

choices.text: The consumers are reading a cached version of the dataset and should refresh their browsers to see the missing rows again
The platform automatically expired yesterday's rows because they were older than the dataset's default retention period
Today's run wrote a SNAPSHOT of only new rows, replacing the view; the writer should append, or snapshot the full intended contents
The source deleted the rows overnight and the dataset correctly reflects that deletion, even though the source still shows them

stem: A streaming pipeline must join each event with the latest customer tier, which changes a few times a year and lives in a dataset. What is a sound approach?

choices.text: Copy the customer tier into every event at the source system so that the streaming pipeline never needs to join at all
Load the customer tiers as a lookup (broadcast state or reference table) refreshed when the dataset updates, joining in-stream
Skip the tier in the stream and add it in a nightly batch, since streaming pipelines cannot use reference data
Query the customer dataset with a full scan for every single event as it arrives, so the tier is always perfectly current

stem: A team must backfill three years of history for a new incremental transform without blocking the daily runs that consumers depend on. What approach is appropriate?

choices.text: Copy three years of output from another team's similar dataset and hope it matches the new logic
Run the three-year backfill as one enormous build on the production branch during business hours and pause daily runs until it ends
Skip the backfill and tell consumers the history starts today
Backfill in validated monthly chunks on a branch or separate schedule, then merge so daily runs continue

stem: A pipeline must build only on business days and only after the upstream finance sync has landed, because finance does not deliver on weekends or public holidays. How should the schedule be configured?

choices.text: A manual build started by an engineer each business morning after checking whether finance has delivered
An input-update trigger on the finance sync, so builds happen when data lands, with freshness checks aware of business days
A fixed daily timer at 06:00 including weekends, with weekend builds simply failing when the finance data is missing
A schedule every fifteen minutes around the clock that force-builds the pipeline regardless of whether the input changed

stem: A transform's runtime suddenly doubled. Job Comparison shows identical stages, but one stage now spends most of its time in garbage collection, and executor memory usage is near its limit. Input size is unchanged. What is likely and what should be done?

choices.text: The cluster is busier than usual today, so the build should simply be rerun later without any investigation
The build identity's permissions changed and the platform is retrying reads in the background
A memory-heavy change (wider rows, a large cached object) is causing GC pressure; find it and reduce memory use
The input dataset has too many files and should be compacted before the next build runs

stem: An engineer discovers that a scheduled pipeline has been failing silently for a week because its failure alerts were routed to a person who left the company. What should be fixed?

choices.text: Route alerts to a team rotation instead of a person, record ownership, and review routing periodically
Disable alerts for the pipeline, since nobody noticed the failures for a week and they must not matter
Add more people individually to the alert list so that at least one of them is likely to still work at the company
Re-route the alerts to the engineer who discovered the issue, since they now know about the pipeline

stem: After a pipeline was moved to a new project, its scheduled builds stopped running, although the code and datasets are intact. What should be checked?

choices.text: Whether the transform code needs to be rewritten for the new project, since code written in one project cannot run in another
Whether the platform pauses all schedules for a week after any project move as a safety measure
Whether the datasets need to be deleted and recreated in the new project for the schedule to recognize them
Whether the schedule and its build identity survived the move and still have access to inputs and outputs

stem: A heavy pipeline and an urgent ad hoc analysis compete for the same compute every morning. The pipeline must finish by 08:00; the analysis is needed by noon. How should this be handled?

choices.text: Run both at 06:00 with maximum resources so that both finish as early as possible regardless of contention
Run the analysis first since it is urgent, and let the pipeline finish whenever it can
Cancel the analysis permanently because pipelines always take precedence over analysts
Run the deadline-bound pipeline first or on reserved capacity, then the analysis, verifying both deadlines

stem: A data engineer wants to understand why a dataset built today is slower than the same build last week. Which tool directly compares the two runs?

choices.text: The user access audit log, which lists who opened the dataset during the week
Job Comparison, which compares the two builds' stages, durations, volumes and resources side by side
The Ontology Manager, which shows how each object type was indexed after the build finished
The dataset's description field, which records performance notes added by previous engineers over time
