stem: A team wants to release pipeline changes weekly with minimal risk. Which release practice fits?

choices.text: Release changes only on Friday evenings so that problems surface over the weekend when fewer people use the data
Collect all changes for three months and release them together in one large merge to minimize the number of releases
Branch per change with branch builds and output comparison, reviewed merges, release notes and rollback
Merge every change directly into main as soon as it is written, since small changes cannot cause problems

stem: An on-call engineer finds that a critical dataset failed to build because one of twelve inputs is stale; the other eleven are fresh. Consumers need today's data by 09:00. What is the best response?

choices.text: Diagnose the stale input; if unfixable in time, let the owner choose a caveated publish or the last good version
Delete the stale input dataset so that the build stops depending on it and succeeds every day from now on
Wait silently until the stale input recovers on its own, however long that takes, without informing anyone
Rebuild the dataset ignoring the stale input entirely, without telling consumers that one source is missing from today's figures

stem: An orders dataset must satisfy: every order has exactly one customer, the order total equals the sum of its line items within one cent, and order dates are not in the future. Where should these rules be enforced?

choices.text: As notes in the dataset description so that consumers know which rules the data is supposed to satisfy
As build-blocking expectations on the curated dataset, with the line sum computed in the transform and asserted
As health checks on the published dataset that alert the owner after consumers have already received the data for the day
As a weekly manual review by an analyst who samples a few orders and compares them against the source system by hand

stem: An expectation began failing every night after a source started sending a small number of legitimately negative quantities (returns). The expectation requires quantity > 0. What should be done?

choices.text: Remove the expectation entirely so that the nightly builds stop failing on the returns
Filter out all negative quantities in the transform before the expectation runs so that the nightly build passes again
Ask the on-call engineer to override the expectation manually every night
Update the contract: allow negative quantities for return rows only, keep the rule for sales, and add a test case

stem: A dataset should receive roughly 50,000 rows per weekday and 5,000 on weekends. A team wants to be alerted when a day's volume is abnormal. Which configuration is appropriate?

choices.text: An alert whenever the row count differs from yesterday's count by any amount at all
A fixed alert whenever the row count is below 50,000, which will fire every weekend but is simple to configure
A size check with day-of-week expected ranges or same-weekday history, alerting beyond a tolerance
No volume monitoring, since row counts naturally vary and alerts would be noisy

stem: Which statement best describes when to choose a build-blocking expectation over an alert-only check?

choices.text: Block when a violation would harm consumers and has no legitimate exceptions; alert when it may be legitimate
Always choose blocking, because any data problem should stop the pipeline until a person has reviewed it
Always choose alert-only, because blocking builds causes outages that are worse than bad data
Choose randomly, since both mechanisms provide the same protection in practice

stem: A health check on the number of distinct customers per day dropped by 40% overnight, but total rows are unchanged. What does this suggest and how should it be investigated?

choices.text: The number of distinct customers per day is not a meaningful quality metric and should never have been monitored at all
The health check is broken and should be deleted because totals did not change
Customer ids were likely collapsed (a placeholder or overwriting join); check the id distribution and upstream changes
Customer behaviour changed overnight and nothing technical needs to be checked

stem: A pipeline needs to publish a dataset daily even when a small fraction of rows fail validation, but consumers must never see invalid rows. What design meets both requirements?

choices.text: Fail the whole build whenever any single row fails validation, regardless of how many of the other rows are perfectly valid
Route valid rows to the curated output and invalid rows to a rejects dataset with reasons, capping the reject rate
Fix invalid rows automatically by replacing bad values with defaults so that every row passes
Publish everything and flag invalid rows with a column that consumers are asked to filter on

stem: Which monitoring combination most quickly detects that a curated dataset is complete in rows but wrong in a key business total?

choices.text: Reconciliation of the dataset's total against an independent source control total, plus amount distribution checks
A row-count check with a tight tolerance on the curated dataset, since completeness implies correctness
A freshness check on the curated dataset that alerts if the data is older than one day
A schema check and a build-status check on the curated dataset, which together cover structure and success

stem: A critical dataset has 25 expectations, and the team finds that builds fail several times a week on expectations that turn out to be too strict, delaying consumers. What is a balanced response?

choices.text: Remove all expectations so that the builds never fail again
Add more expectations so that real problems are more likely to be caught among the false ones
Ignore failures by configuring the pipeline to publish even when expectations fail
Review each failing rule against the contract: keep true invariants, relax or convert wrong ones to alerts, document

stem: A dataset contains salary data. Only HR and payroll may read it. A derived dataset aggregates average salary by department with at least 20 employees per group, intended for all managers. How should markings be handled?

choices.text: Publish the aggregate with no review, since aggregates are never sensitive in any circumstance
Keep the source marked; after a documented review that the aggregate cannot reveal individuals, publish it unmarked
Apply the salary marking to both datasets so that only HR and payroll can read the aggregate as well
Remove the marking from the salary dataset so that the aggregation pipeline can run under any identity

stem: A new analyst joins the marketing team and needs read access to the team's curated datasets but nothing else. What is the cleanest way to grant it?

choices.text: Grant Viewer on each marketing dataset individually to the analyst's personal account, one dataset at a time
Grant the analyst Owner on every project in the organization so that they never encounter a permission error
Add the analyst to the marketing consumers group that already holds Viewer on the marketing curated project
Share an existing team member's credentials with the analyst until permanent access is arranged

stem: After a restricted view's policy was updated to add a new region, users from an existing region report seeing no rows at all. What is the likely cause?

choices.text: The edit introduced a logic error (AND instead of OR, a mistyped attribute); test the policy with users from each region
The underlying dataset was deleted at the same time the policy was updated
The users' browsers need to be restarted after any policy change
Restricted views can only support one region condition at a time, so adding a second region automatically breaks the first

stem: An auditor asks which identities could read a sensitive dataset at any time during the last quarter. What evidence should the data engineer provide?

choices.text: A screenshot of the project's sharing settings taken at the end of the quarter
A statement from the project owner that only the right people had access throughout the quarter
The current list of users who can read the dataset today, which should reflect the last quarter's access closely enough
Role, group and marking membership history for the quarter, with access logs showing actual reads

stem: A data engineer is explaining to a new team member what happens to sensitivity when marked data flows through pipelines into other projects. Which statement about how markings propagate is correct?

choices.text: Markings propagate only to datasets in the same project as the marked source
Markings follow data through lineage into derived datasets, unless deliberately removed after review
Markings propagate only when a user manually copies them to each derived dataset
Markings apply only to the dataset they are placed on and never to any dataset derived from it by a transform

stem: A team wants to give a third-party vendor access to one curated dataset for a six-week integration project. Which approach balances need and risk?

choices.text: Copy the dataset to the vendor's systems without any record of the transfer
Refuse any access, since vendors should never see company data
Time-bound Viewer access through a dedicated group on a project holding only the needed dataset, with expiry
Add the vendor's users to the organization permanently with Viewer on all curated projects so future projects are easier

stem: A restricted view must hide rows for customers who opted out of analytics from everyone except the privacy team. The opt-out flag is in a separate consent dataset. How should this be built?

choices.text: Add a column named "do_not_use" and trust that analysts will respect it
Delete opted-out customers from the source system entirely so that their records never reach the platform at all
Ask analysts to remember to filter out opted-out customers in every query they run
Join consent into the view's backing dataset and write a policy showing opted-out rows only to the privacy team

stem: A build identity has accumulated access to 300 datasets over two years, although the pipeline now reads only 12. What risk does this create and what should be done?

choices.text: Excess privilege widens the blast radius; trim grants to the 12 inputs and outputs, verify on a branch, review regularly
No risk; extra access is harmless as long as the pipeline's code does not read the other datasets
Rename the identity so that it is less likely to be misused
Delete the build identity and create a new one with administrator rights so permission problems never occur

stem: A hospital system models Patients, Doctors and Appointments. An appointment involves one patient and one doctor at a specific time, and applications must list a doctor's appointments and a patient's history. Which model is correct?

choices.text: A single Patient object per appointment, so that each visit creates a new patient record holding the doctor and time
A many-to-many link between Patient and Doctor with no properties, with appointment times stored as a list on the Patient object
Appointment times stored as a list property on each Doctor object, with patient names in a parallel list in the same order
An Appointment object type with time and status, linked many-to-one to Patient and to Doctor

stem: An object type uses an email address as its primary key. Customers sometimes change their email, and when they do, their history disappears from the application. What is the cause and the fix?

choices.text: The application caches old objects; clearing the cache will restore each customer's history after an email change
Email is mutable, so a change re-keys the object and detaches history and edits; switch to a stable id and migrate
The pipeline is dropping rows with new emails; adding a filter on email format will prevent the loss
Customers should be told never to change their email address in the source system

stem: Analysts want a "Top 10 products this week" list in a dashboard. A colleague proposes a TopProduct object type rebuilt weekly with ranks 1–10. What is the better modeling approach?

choices.text: Create ten separate object types, one for each rank position, each holding one product reference
Store the top-10 list as a text property on a single global object that the dashboard reads and parses
Keep Product as the entity with a weekly sales metric (or a ProductWeek type) and rank in the dashboard
Create the TopProduct object type as proposed, since it is the fastest way to make the dashboard work for analysts this week

stem: A team needs to split an existing object type "Asset" into two types, "Vehicle" and "Building", because their properties diverge. Applications and edits exist on Asset. How should the change be made?

choices.text: On a branch, create both types, migrate edits and links, update the applications, then merge together
Keep a single Asset type and add every property of both, leaving most of them empty on each object
Delete the Asset type and create the two new types from scratch, accepting the loss of user edits and links
Create the new types in production immediately and tell application owners to switch whenever they can

stem: Which property design is most appropriate for a "status" field that applications filter on and that must take one of five values?

choices.text: A numeric property where each status is encoded as an arbitrary number known only to the engineers
A free-text string property where each pipeline writes whatever wording its source system uses for the status
Five separate boolean properties, one per status, with applications checking which one is true
A string property constrained to an enumerated set (or a value type), validated by an expectation in the pipeline

stem: An application shows each customer's lifetime revenue. Recomputing it from all orders on every page view is slow. The value only needs to be current to the previous day. Where should it be computed?

choices.text: South, as a property materialized by the daily pipeline from the orders data, so pages read a stored value
In the browser by downloading all of the customer's orders and summing them on the user's device
North of the Ontology in a function on every page view, accepting the slowness so the value is always perfectly current
By the customer service team, who update the value manually when a customer asks about it

stem: Two source systems describe the same physical Warehouse with different ids. Applications need one Warehouse object. How should the backing data be modeled?

choices.text: Use the warehouse name as the key, since both systems spell the names similarly most of the time
Create two Warehouse objects, one per source, and let users figure out which one to use in each case
Map each source id to one canonical id through a crosswalk, key the object on it, keep source ids as properties
Concatenate both source ids into one string key so that both are represented in the single object

stem: After a backing dataset was rebuilt with a corrected join, the number of objects of a type dropped by 5%, and some users report missing objects they had edited. What should the engineer do?

choices.text: Restore the old, incorrect join permanently so that no objects ever disappear again
Diff the key sets, classify removed keys, restore legitimate objects and their edits, and add a key-churn check
Accept the change, since the corrected join is more accurate and the missing objects were probably wrong
Ask users to recreate the missing objects and their edits by hand

stem: A data engineer wants help writing a complex window-function transform but needs the result to be correct on real data. Which workflow uses AI assistance appropriately?

choices.text: Ask a code assistant for the transform and merge it directly, since assistants are trained on large amounts of correct window-function code
Avoid AI assistance entirely, since generated code can never be trusted for data transformations of any kind
Ask an LLM transform inside the pipeline to compute the window values for each row at runtime instead of writing code
Use a code assistant to draft the transform, then review it, add unit tests on edge cases, and compare a branch build against expectations

stem: An LLM extraction transform shows a slowly rising share of rows with empty outputs over several weeks, while schema checks pass. What should the engineer investigate?

choices.text: Whether inputs or the model changed; sample empty rows, read traces and raw responses, and add an empty-rate check
Whether the prompt is too short, and if so make it much longer without examining any failing rows
Whether the dataset's storage is running out, since empty outputs indicate the platform could not write values
Nothing, since empty outputs are valid strings and therefore pass every check in the pipeline

stem: A team wants to classify incoming support tickets into categories for routing. Volume is 20,000 tickets a day and categories must be available within minutes of a ticket's creation. Which placement and design fit?

choices.text: An agent that classifies each ticket only when a support worker opens it, so the classification is always as current as possible
An event-driven step classifying each new ticket into validated categories, stored as a property for routing
A manual classification queue where support staff categorize each ticket before routing
A nightly batch classifying the day's tickets, so routing happens the next morning

stem: A code assistant proposes replacing a well-tested deduplication transform with a "simpler" version. What should the engineer require before accepting it?

choices.text: Approval from a stakeholder who does not read code but likes simpler solutions
A promise from the assistant that the new version is equivalent
Proof of equivalence: existing tests pass, branch output matches production by key, and edge cases agree
Nothing, because simpler code is always better, and the assistant has already reviewed the original logic and its tests in detail

stem: Which output configuration for an LLM transform best supports downstream joins on the extracted field?

choices.text: An output that includes the field inside a natural sentence such as "The supplier mentioned here is ACME Corp." for readability
A numeric confidence score only, from which the field can be inferred later
A typed field normalized to the join key format and validated against the reference dataset it joins to
Free-text output that downstream transforms parse with string matching before joining

stem: An LLM enrichment step is accurate but costly. The team notices that 60% of inputs are near-identical boilerplate texts. What optimization preserves quality while reducing cost?

choices.text: Switch to the cheapest available model for all rows without evaluating whether quality is still acceptable
Process only a random 40% of rows each night and leave the others without an enrichment value
Remove the enrichment entirely because the cost cannot be justified for any of the rows
Normalize inputs, cache results by normalized content and prompt version, and call the model only on misses

stem: A code assistant generated a transform that reads an entire upstream dataset every run, although the upstream is append-only and the transform only needs new rows. The pipeline is slow and expensive. What should the engineer change?

choices.text: Reduce the upstream dataset by deleting old rows so that the full read is smaller
Rewrite it as incremental over the append-only input, validated on a branch for identical results
Increase the number of executors so the full read finishes faster each night
Accept the full read, since code generated by an assistant can be assumed to be optimal for the platform it targets

stem: A manager proposes that an AI agent should automatically create new pipelines whenever a business user asks for a dataset in chat. What should the data engineer advise?

choices.text: Let the AI draft a proposal for engineering review, with branch validation, ownership and governance before publishing
Refuse to use AI anywhere in the data request process
Agree, since automatically generated pipelines will reduce the backlog of data requests immediately
Agree but only for requests that involve sensitive data, since those are the most urgent

stem: A new source must be onboarded: an on-premises database behind a firewall, a table of 400 million rows with a reliable update timestamp and soft deletes, needed daily by finance. Which end-to-end ingestion design is appropriate?

choices.text: An agent, an initial snapshot then a daily update sync with lookback, soft deletes applied, and freshness checks
A weekly manual export by the database team to a shared drive, uploaded by an analyst to the platform on Monday mornings
A direct connection from the platform through a temporary firewall opening, running a full snapshot of the whole table every night with no checks
A streaming CDC pipeline with second-level latency, since streaming is always preferable for large tables

stem: A critical transform computes revenue recognition. A new engineer must change one rule. Which combination of safeguards should already be in place so the change cannot silently corrupt revenue?

choices.text: A lock that prevents anyone from ever editing the transform again after its first release
A monthly check by finance of whether the revenue numbers look roughly right compared with last month
Unit tests on the rules, reconciliation expectations, branch comparison with production, and required review
A comment at the top of the transform asking engineers to be careful when they edit revenue logic

stem: A team must choose a processing design for an append-only event dataset of 50 billion rows that grows daily, with consumers needing daily aggregates and occasional late events up to 7 days old. Which design fits?

choices.text: A streaming pipeline with no persistence, since streaming always handles late data automatically without any configuration
An incremental transform that ignores late events entirely, since they are only a small fraction of all events
A full nightly batch over all 50 billion rows, since full recomputation always handles late events correctly
Incremental over new appends, partitioned by event date, recomputing the last 7 days, with periodic reconciliation

stem: A critical dataset failed at 03:00. The on-call engineer must restore service by 07:00 and prevent recurrence. Which sequence reflects the full operational playbook?

choices.text: Force-rebuild everything upstream repeatedly until something succeeds, then go back to sleep without recording anything
Locate the first failing stage, classify it, repair minimally, verify, inform consumers, then add a guarding check
Roll back every dataset in the pipeline to last week's version so that consumers see consistent data
Wait for the next scheduled run, since most failures resolve themselves overnight without intervention

stem: A curated dataset feeds both a regulatory report and an exploratory dashboard. The regulatory report needs strict correctness; the dashboard tolerates small gaps but wants daily freshness. How should quality controls be arranged?

choices.text: A shared validated base, a strictly gated regulatory output, and a dashboard output that publishes daily with alerts
Separate pipelines from raw data for each consumer with independent logic and no shared base
No expectations at all, so that the dashboard is always fresh and the regulatory team checks the report by hand
One strict expectation set on a single dataset, accepting that the dashboard goes stale whenever the regulatory checks fail

stem: A dataset containing personal data feeds an Ontology object type used by a customer-service app, an analytics dataset for marketing, and an export to a partner. A review must confirm protection along every path. What should the review cover?

choices.text: A survey asking each consuming team whether they believe they handle the data correctly
Only the partner export, since external sharing is the only path that can expose personal data
Every lineage path: markings on derived data and objects, view policies, roles, export policy and identity scopes
Only the source dataset's marking, since everything downstream is protected automatically by that one control

stem: A team is designing the backing dataset for a new "Shipment" object type fed by three carriers with overlapping tracking numbers. Applications need stable objects, links to Orders, and user edits that survive daily rebuilds. Which design decisions are essential?

choices.text: Use the tracking number alone as the key, since carriers promise their numbers are unique within their own systems
Store all three carriers' data in three separate Shipment object types so that keys never collide
Rebuild the object type from scratch daily with new random keys so that no stale objects ever remain
A carrier-namespaced key with a uniqueness expectation, one row per key, a validated Order link, and churn monitoring

stem: Leadership asks the data engineering team to add AI-generated summaries to every record in a 10-million-row dataset nightly. Only about 2% of records change daily, and summaries are read mostly in one application. What is the most responsible design?

choices.text: Refuse the request because AI summaries cannot be made reliable for production data
Generate incrementally for changed rows with caching, validated output and version columns, reviewing on-demand placement
Generate summaries only for a random 1% sample to control cost and leave the rest empty
Generate summaries for all 10 million rows every night so that they are always perfectly consistent with each other
